title: Jason Alexander apologizes after Courtney Stodden says 2012 comedy sketch objectified her as a minor
summary: Jason Alexander apologized to Courtney Stodden after she shared a photo from a 2012 sketch where he rubbed a cellphone across her chest when she was 17.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Jason Alexander is taking accountability for his past mistakes.

The 66-year-old actor recently apologized to Courtney Stodden for participating in a 2012 Funny or Die sketch in which he held a cellphone up to her chest and made comments about her body when she was a minor.

"Looking back at the comedy sketch in which Ms. Stodden and I participated in 2012, I completely agree that it was inappropriate and I truly regret it," he told Fox News Digital in a statement. "But more importantly, I am deeply sorry for any harm or distress it has caused Ms. Stodden. I offer her my sincerest apologies."
His apology comes one day after Stodden called out Alexander on Instagram as one of the writers of the sketch, adding, "As an adult, that fact has become harder—not easier—for me to understand."
GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'
Alexander apologized to Stodden for a 2012 sketch in which he objectified her body. (Getty Images)
In the Instagram post, she shared a photo of her and Alexander in the sketch, in which she is wearing a bikini, and the actor is rubbing a cellphone across her chest.

"I was 17 years old in this photo. The older I get, the more impossible this is to understand," she wrote. "During this comedy sketch, Jason Alexander repeatedly rubbed his phone across my breasts while saying there was 'no signal' in my head but 'plenty of signal' in my chest. Later in the sketch, he joked that when I turned 18 he’d like to take me behind the couch and 'have his way' with me."
She added that as a minor she "didn’t have the legal power to decide whether I wanted to participate" and that "the contracts were signed by adults."
At the time, she was married to Doug Hutchison, who she tied the knot with when she was 16 and he was 51, noting the paycheck for this appearance went to him.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Stodden described feeling alone while on the set of Funny or Die. (Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty Images)

"I was the only child in the room. I felt so alone," she added. "Looking back now, I don’t see comedy. I see a 17-year-old girl whose body became part of an adult joke. People still say, 'You chose to be there.' Legally, I couldn’t make those decisions for myself. That’s the point."
She ended the post by acknowledging that while she isn't able to change what she went through, she finds herself asking, "How did so many adults look at a minor and decide this was acceptable?"
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
"That’s exactly why I speak out today," she concluded. "Children deserve laws that protect them. They shouldn’t have to become adults before realizing the law should have protected them all along."

The caption also included a call to support California Assembly Bill 1267, which aims to permanently end child marriage by setting the minimum legal age for marriage in California to 18 with no exceptions.
Stodden married Hutchison when she was 16 and he was 51, and is now advocating for legislation banning child marriage without exception. (JB Lacroix/WireImage)

Stodden and Hutchison got married in 2011 despite their 34-year age gap. They split up and got back together a few times before officially calling it quits in 2016, although divorce papers were not filed until March 2018, with the divorce being finalized in March 2020.
She announced their divorce in an Instagram post featuring her wedding photo, calling it "an emotional day," but assured her fans "it’s for the better."
Stodden announced her divorce on Instagram in March 2020, saying in the caption she now feels taken advantage of. (Tibrina Hobson/Getty Images)

"I look back at this picture and feel absolutely taken advantage of," she wrote. "I’ve been scared to even speak up about feeling groomed or being verbally abused during the almost 10 year marriage because I was a child and he was 50 when we married but I’m a woman now and it’s time for me to put my big girl pants on and speak on this matter."
She continued: "I’ve felt completely trapped, manipulated and at times abandoned by adults // growing up in such an environment — it became a lonely and dark place."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

title: Lil Wayne praises Trump's White House ballroom project, calls out critics who 'don't know nothing'
summary: Lil Wayne says critics "don't know nothing" about why Trump's White House ballroom is needed after his own experience performing for Kamala Harris
story: President Donald Trump gives an exclusive tour of the White House Ballroom project, highlighting its design, immense capacity and enhanced security features. He emphasizes it's a gift to America for future generations.
Lil Wayne is throwing his support behind one of President Donald Trump's most talked-about White House projects.

The rap icon praised Trump's plan to build a massive White House ballroom during a Monday appearance on the "Friends Keep Secrets" podcast, arguing the new venue would spare performers from being pushed outside for major events.

"I'm so glad to hear Trump say — when they was mad at him about building the ballroom, and he was like, 'Because everything we do we have to do it on the damn lawn," Wayne, whose real name is Dwayne Michael Carter Jr., said.
KAI TRUMP REVEALS NEW CELEBRITY CRUSH AFTER DITCHING 'OUTER BANKS' STAR DREW STARKEY
The rapper praised Trump's White House ballroom plan, saying he was glad to hear the president push for the upgrade. (Greg Doherty / Getty Images for 2K; Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images)
"So, people who don't know nothing [are] hearing that thinking he's just being Trump — no, for real, I was glad to hear him saying that," he added.
Wayne's praise stemmed from a memorable performance he gave at then-Vice President Kamala Harris' 2023 celebration marking the 50th anniversary of hip-hop.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Lil Wayne said that a 2023 Kamala Harris hip-hop anniversary performance felt like a "backyard barbecue." (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)
TRUMP CLAIMS DONOR FUNDED WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM INCLUDES HIDDEN BUILD BELOW WITH SECURITY FOCUS
The event unfolded outside at Number One Observatory Circle, where the rapper said it felt like he was attending a "backyard barbecue."

Trump has repeatedly pitched the ballroom as a long-overdue upgrade for the White House, arguing it would provide a permanent indoor venue for state dinners, diplomatic receptions, performances and other major events while enhancing security for high-profile gatherings.
Lil Wayne said he was confused when he arrived for the performance, admitting he thought he was heading inside the actual White House. (Erika Goldring/Getty Images)
In a Truth Social post in May, Trump said the ballroom is "going up rapidly" on the east side of the White House and dismissed reports of ballooning costs.

President Donald Trump holds design for a proposed White House ballroom while speaking to reporters. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg)

He argued the project grew in price only because it was redesigned to be "approximately twice the size, and a far higher quality, than the original proposal," which he said, "would not have been adequate to handle the necessary events, meetings, and even future Inaugurations."

Trump said the original proposal carried a $200 million price tag, while the expanded project "will be something less than 400 Million Dollars."

title: 'Dutton Ranch' star Ed Harris blasts producers, says he wanted to void contract: 'Get me the f--- out'
summary: Ed Harris says he felt "misled" about his role in "Dutton Ranch" and told his team to get him out before production wrapped on the first season.
story: The "Dutton Ranch" star reflects on his family’s deep ties to Montana as the Paramount+ series premieres May 15 with two episodes, followed by weekly releases.
Ed Harris says he came close to walking away from Taylor Sheridan's "Dutton Ranch."
The veteran actor revealed he felt "underused and inconsequential" while filming the show's first season, prompting him to tell his team to "get me the f--- out of here" before production wrapped.

"Prior to signing on for it, I was talked to quite a bit about what the season was, and what my character was going to do — and that I was one of the four main characters," Harris told Variety. "And that wasn't really the case."
COLE HAUSER SAYS HIS FAMILY HELPED SHAPE MONTANA AS FANS FOLLOW TAYLOR SHERIDAN FROM TREASURE STATE TO TEXAS
Ed Harris says he nearly quit Taylor Sheridan's "Dutton Ranch." (Emerson Miller/Paramount+.)

The Oscar-nominated actor, who plays veterinarian Everett McKinney in the "Yellowstone" spin-off, said he felt "misled" about the importance of his character after allegedly being promised a much larger role before production began.
By the middle of filming, Harris said he'd reached his breaking point.
Harris said he confronted the production about his concerns, though he did not identify Sheridan by name.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Harris is seen with Kelly Reilly as Beth Dutton in "Dutton Ranch." (Emerson Miller/Paramount+)

"I said, 'I'm feeling underused and inconsequential,' and they kind of went, 'Oh,'" Harris said. "I'm being told my character will have a little bit more to do [in Season 2]. I was just a little frustrated, to tell you the truth."
Looking back after watching the finished season, Harris admitted his perspective changed.
He called "Dutton Ranch" "pretty good" and said Everett ended up feeling "relatively important to the story." Still, he said that wasn't how it felt while cameras were rolling.
A cut musical scene left Harris fuming at "Dutton Ranch" producers, saying it was "enough reason" to void his contract with the show. (Emerson Miller/Paramount+)
Harris said he filmed a sequence in which Everett is invited to sing in a bar — only to discover it had been axed from production.

"So, there's this scene in there … I'm talking to [Beth Dutton] at the bar, and [Rip Wheeler] comes in and says, 'OK, Everett, come on, it's your turn,'" Harris said. "I walk up to the mic, and they cut it… They cut the song out. I'm going, 'F--- you, people.'"
According to Harris, producers told him the musical moment was removed because it was "too 'up' for the dark ending of that episode."
Harris said he felt that was "enough reason to say I'm voiding my contract."

Despite his blunt remarks, Harris remains signed on for two seasons of "Dutton Ranch," and it remains unclear whether he is seriously considering leaving the series.
Harris revealed he felt "underused" filming "Dutton Ranch" and nearly voided his contract on the Taylor Sheridan "Yellowstone" spinoff. (Omar Vega/Getty Images)
Sheridan's latest chapter in the "Yellowstone" universe debuted on Paramount+ in May.

The series picks up with fan favorites Beth Dutton (Kelly Reilly) and Rip Wheeler (Cole Hauser) as they trade Montana for South Texas, where they're determined to build a ranch — and a new life — from the ground up.

title: Angelina Jolie achieves 'complete cutting of ties' between kids and Brad Pitt as twins turn 18: expert
summary: Five of Brad Pitt's children have dropped his surname as a family law expert says Angelina Jolie achieved the "complete cutting of ties" she sought.
story: Jon Voight spoke to Fox News Digital while promoting his film "Reagan," and weighed in on the family drama between his daughter Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt.
A decade after one of Hollywood's most bitter divorces began, Angelina Jolie has finally achieved a "complete cutting of ties" with ex-husband Brad Pitt.

With the former couple's youngest children now 18, the last legal thread connecting Jolie and Pitt has effectively been severed, a family law expert explained to Fox News Digital. The expert argued the Oscar winner has reached the outcome she had been seeking since filing for divorce in 2016.

"For those that followed the Pitt/Jolie divorce since 2016, it should be no surprise that Angelina Jolie is finally able to achieve what she attempted to get in the 2016 divorce — a complete cutting of ties between the children and Brad Pitt," Holly Davis, cofounder of Kirker Davis LLP, told Fox News Digital.
BRAD PITT FACES FRESH FAMILY BLOW AS DAUGHTER CLEARS MAJOR HURDLE TO DROP HIS LAST NAME

Angelina Jolie has achieved what one family law expert described as a "complete cutting of ties" between ex-husband Brad Pitt and their kids after the former couple's youngest children turned 18. (Toni Anne Barson Archive/WireImage)
Pitt and Jolie share six children: Maddox, Zahara, Shiloh, Pax, Knox and Vivienne.
Twins Knox and Vivienne reaching adulthood on July 12 means custody issues are no longer before the court, giving Jolie the freedom to make decisions that previously required court oversight.

"Because she was unable to achieve this result in the parties' divorce, she had to wait until the youngest children were 18 to be able to do the things that the court would not allow her to do," Davis explained.
What ultimately drove the children's estrangement from their father remains impossible to know from the outside, according to Davis.

"Whether or not she influenced them in hating their father based on the legitimate problems in her romantic relationship with Brad, or whether they all suffered similar difficult moments as a family which lead to their decision to no longer see him, will be anyone's guess," the family attorney said.

Jolie and Pitt's daughter Vivienne is seeking to remove "Pitt" legally from her last name — from Vivienne Marcheline Jolie-Pitt to Vivienne Marcheline Jolie — just over a week after turning 18, according to People magazine.
The petition was filed in Los Angeles County Superior Court, with the reason for the name change noted as "personal," per the outlet, with the hearing scheduled for November 2.

Two years prior, Vivienne worked on the Broadway play "The Outsiders" with mom Angelina, and was credited as "Vivienne Jolie" in the playbill. Vivienne worked as a producer assistant on the musical while Angelina served as a producer.
Family law and entertainment experts are divided over whether Brad Pitt's strained relationship with several of his children will have any lasting impact on the actor's public image. (Getty Images)
BRAD PITT FIGHTS FOR SURVIVAL IN 'HEART OF THE BEAST' TRAILER AS FANS SAY HE'S 'COOLER' THAN YOUNGER ACTORS
Jolie may have effectively severed the remaining legal family ties, but experts say the public fallout might not significantly damage Pitt's Hollywood standing.

"Brandwise, it’s not that big of a hit to Brad Pitt’s name or brand," entertainment attorney Tre Lovell told Fox News Digital. "He’s such a universally well-known star, and his divorce with Angelina Jolie and strained relationship with his kids have been well publicized."

"Most of the public would chalk it up to an unfortunate problem with the relationship with his kids, but as far as his brand, it’s still strong and would survive any type of criticism in this area," the lawyer for Los Angeles-based Lovell Firm explained.

Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie's yearslong family divide has entered a new chapter as legal experts weigh in on what their twins reaching adulthood means for the former couple. (Jason LaVeris/FilmMagic via Getty)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Five of Pitt and Jolie's children have distanced themselves from the actor by dropping his surname, with Vivienne and three of her siblings choosing to make the change official legally.

"[Pitt's] talent remains unquestioned. But when multiple adult children publicly choose to stop using your surname, the conversation inevitably shifts from career to character," crisis communications expert Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital. "Whether fair or unfair, that’s the kind of narrative no amount of good publicity can easily overcome."
Four of Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt's kids have made moves to legally drop the actor's surname. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

Zahara filed to formally remove "Pitt" from her surname in June. If granted, her legal name will change from Zahara Marley Jolie-Pitt to Zahara Marley Jolie. Her name change follows Shiloh's name change in 2024. Maddox also reportedly filed a petition in May.

"This isn’t about a single family decision… it’s about accumulation," he added. "One child dropping a famous last name might be dismissed as an isolated event. When it happens repeatedly across multiple adult children, it stops looking like celebrity gossip and starts becoming part of a public figure’s legacy."
Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt finalized their divorce in 2024, but experts say the former couple's highly public family conflict continues to generate headlines. (STR/AFP via Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Experts told Fox News Digital that Brad Pitt's Hollywood brand remains strong despite renewed attention on his relationship with his children and ex-wife Angelina Jolie. (Getty Images)

The public's reaction to the family drama, however, remains open to interpretation. While some experts believe the repeated rejection of Pitt's surname could become part of his public legacy, others contend the developments may instead generate sympathy for the Oscar-winning actor.

"One of the primary things that parents should focus on in a divorce is the well-being of the child, and that often means striving for the child to have a healthy relationship with both parents," Jordan Matthews told Fox News Digital.

The entertainment attorney for Los Angeles-based Holtz Matthews LLP argued that while the decision to drop Pitt's last name was "highly personal," it is likely to leave many members of the public "sympathetic to Pitt’s position."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

title: Prince William, Kate Middleton wrestled with major decision over Prince George's future: expert
summary: Prince George passed Eton College entrance exams with "no special treatment," as Prince William and Kate Middleton reportedly debated the boarding school choice.
story: Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair royal correspondent and co-host of "The Royals Uncensored," says Prince George passed Eton's admissions process like other applicants before accepting his place at the prestigious school.
Prince William and Kate Middleton wrestled with a major decision about Prince George's future.

Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair's royal correspondent and co-host of "The Royals Uncensored," first reported that Prince George received "no special treatment" and had to pass Eton College's entrance exams just like every other applicant.
Kensington Palace recently announced that George, who turns 13 on July 22, will attend the prestigious boarding school where his father and uncle, Prince Harry, were educated.
PRINCE WILLIAM AND KATE MIDDLETON 'CAUTIOUS' ABOUT WHICH ROYAL APPEARANCES THEIR CHILDREN MAKE: SOURCE

The Prince and Princess of Wales, seen here on the Isle of Mull, western Scotland, on April 30, 2025, have agreed that their eldest, Prince George, will attend Eton College. (Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images)

"I had been reporting for a while that Eton was the top choice," Nicholl told Fox News Digital. "Although behind the scenes, I think there was a bit of yo-yoing about whether it was the right choice. You've got to remember that George will one day be king. And, of course, William and Catherine are thinking about the future. They're thinking about creating a very modern monarchy that feels relevant."
Eton College Chapel is the main place of worship for students at Eton College, a famous English boys' school. (Mark Kerrison/In Pictures via Getty Images)

"One of the things they were discussing was whether Eton was the right choice because it’s very much traditional, steeped in years of history and heritage and very much seen as an ‘old boys’ club.’ They weren’t sure if that was the right look for Prince George, or at least Catherine had her reservations."

Nicholl reported that Kate was initially "on the fence" about Eton. On her "short list" was her alma mater, the coed Marlborough College. However, "it is understood that, from the outset, William was very keen for his eldest son to be educated at Eton."
WATCH: PRINCE GEORGE EARNED ETON COLLEGE SPOT WITH ‘NO SPECIAL TREATMENT’: EXPERT
Fox News Digital reached out to Kensington Palace for comment.

"I think that on this one, William was pushing hard for Eton, and they did flip-flop over the issue of where to send George," royal expert Charlotte Griffiths told Nicholl. "Ultimately, it would have been a joint decision, but William always wanted Eton and thinks it's the right place for George. It breeds leaders."
A view of Eton College founded by King Henry VI. (Archive Photos/Getty Images)
British royals expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that Eton College holds particular sentimental value for William.

People magazine previously reported that after William's mother, Princess Diana, died in 1997 at age 36, Eton provided stability for the grieving prince. He also developed a close bond with housemaster Andrew Gailey, and several friends from Eton remain close members of his inner circle.
Prince William stands at Eton College in Eton, United Kingdom, wearing a waistcoat as a member of the elite society group called "Pop." (Tim Graham/Photo Library via Getty Images)
A young Prince Harry is seen here at Eton College. (Tim Graham/Getty Images)

"Eton, being in proximity to Windsor Castle, enabled him to walk over on Sundays for tea or lunch with his beloved grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II," Fordwich explained. "This provided him with a natural and casual way to receive guidance directly from her. No doubt Princess Catherine and Prince William are also anticipating staying close to Prince George in a similar manner."
"Additionally, Eton is well-versed in protecting its students from media scrutiny with global elites in attendance," Fordwich noted.
Boys make their way to classes at Eton College, date unknown. (Christopher Furlong/Getty Images)
According to Nicholl, it was an easy choice for George, who was eager to follow in his father's footsteps.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

HRH Prince William, the Prince of Wales, and Prince George sit in the Royal Box as Jannik Sinner of Italy plays Alexander Zverev of Germany in the Gentlemen's Singles Final at Wimbledon in London, England, on July 12, 2026. (Tim Clayton/Getty Images)
"I revealed in Vanity Fair that he had to sit [through] the assessments and the exams, pass all of those, just like everyone else who applied," said Nicholl.

"There was no special treatment. And I think there is just a sense of great relief that the decision has been made, the place has been accepted, and Prince George will be starting Eton in September. I know that William's absolutely delighted, and George, I'm told, is very proud to be going too."
Prince George of Wales is said to be excited that he'll be attending Eton College in the fall. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"William and George are very close, and William will be making sure George is well-prepared," Griffiths also said in Nicholl's reporting. "They will hunker down and spend the summer together in Norfolk before the big move to Eton. It's an exciting time for them all."

Prince George of Wales watches an RAF flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace after the coronation of King Charles III and Queen Camilla at Westminster Abbey in London, circa 2023. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

Eton College, founded in 1440 by King Henry VI, costs about $80,000 a year, according to People magazine. It has educated generations of leaders, including 20 British prime ministers. It's also where George will likely meet many of his future peers before he becomes king.
Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that Eton is known to teach its pupils "to be leaders, not followers."

Students from Eton College in the Mound Stand react to Harrow students during a cricket match between Eton and Harrow at Lord's Cricket Ground in London, England, on May 10, 2024. (Philip Brown/Getty Images)
"George will make many friends for life," said Turner. "He will also see the value of the school playing a part in a collective of power-based individuals."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Prince William signs in on his first day at Eton College on Sept. 6, 1995. (Anwar Hussein/WireImage)
Other royal experts told Fox News Digital that the Prince and Princess of Wales likely learned lessons from King Charles III's experiences when considering George's future.

"The lessons the royals learned after sending the then-Prince Charles to Cheam and Gordonstoun, both of which he hated, are that balance is required, which William and Catherine are aware of," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital.
Prince Charles enters Gordonstoun school with school president Capt. Ian Tennant on May 2, 1962. (Keystone-France/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)

"It's imperative that the decisions surrounding the futures of their children fit each child's character. George, from what we know, will relish Eton, and it is also near their home at Forest Lodge. Charles was sensitive and sent to a faraway school, which was a bad mistake."
Princess Catherine and Prince George attend the men's singles final at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club in London, England. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)
"Like both of his parents, Prince George is down to earth," Fordwich said. "From what I hear, he's a charming, well-mannered, kind-hearted, yet reserved young man."

Royal author Robert Jobson told the U.K.'s Daily Mail that George is eager to take on the challenge. Jobson reported that George asked his parents if he could try boarding at Lambrook School, where he attends with his younger siblings, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, 8.

Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis are greeted by Headmaster Jonathan Perry upon their arrival at Lambrook School near Ascot in Berkshire on Sept. 7, 2022, on the eve of their first school day. (Jonathan Brady/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

"Prince William and Catherine have consistently tried to remove the unnecessary trappings of royalty while preserving the institution itself," Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

Prince George of Wales, wearing a hat and sunglasses, attends Day 14 of the Wimbledon Tennis Championships at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club in London, England, on July 12, 2026. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)

"They aren't pretending Prince George is an ordinary child," she said. "That would be absurd. But they're also avoiding the sort of visible favoritism that feeds the outdated narrative that royals believe different rules apply to them. It's modernization through restraint rather than reinvention."
Schofield said William and Kate are raising George to embrace responsibility, not royal privilege.

Kate, Princess of Wales, rides with her sons Prince George and Prince Louis in an open-top carriage returning to Buckingham Palace during Trooping the Colour in London on June 13, 2026. (Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP)

"William and Catherine appear determined to teach George that being king is about responsibility, not entitlement," Schofield said. "By denying him unnecessary special treatment now, they're strengthening his credibility decades before he ever wears the crown."
Prince George is seen here with his younger sister Princess Charlotte in London on July 12, 2026. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)

"They understand that the monarchy survives because the public believes the family lives by many of the same rules everyone else does," she continued. "While George will never have a normal life, they seem determined not to manufacture unnecessary exceptions just because they can. That message is politically valuable and, honestly, good parenting."

While Kate may have initially questioned whether Eton was the right fit for her son, the Princess of Wales is now fully behind the decision as she and William continue to prioritize humility over privilege.

Catherine, Princess of Wales, Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Prince George attended the 2026 Easter Matins Service at St. George's Chapel in Windsor, England, on April 5, 2026. (Mark Cuthbert/UK Press/Getty Images)

"There is no avoiding George’s royal lineage," said Fordwich. "Nevertheless, he has been brought up with solid family values. There are zero accounts of him ever behaving in an entitled manner because he hasn’t been pampered at all."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Jelly Roll's daughter fiercely denies cheating rumors, days after divorce from Bunnie Xo finalized
summary: Bailee Ann fiercely denied cheating rumors in a TikTok livestream, days after Jelly Roll's divorce from Bunnie Xo was finalized in Tennessee.
story: Country music singer Jelly Roll isn't afraid to tackle the ‘uncomfortable stuff’ in his marriage to TikTok star Bunnie XO to keep their marriage strong, the ‘Son of a Sinner’ musician shared with Fox News Digital.
Jelly Roll's daughter fiercely defended her family, days after his divorce from Bunnie Xo was finalized.
Bailee Ann, 18, staunchly denied infidelity rumors between the former couple during a TikTok livestream Sunday.
The "Son of a Sinner" singer petitioned Tennessee courts for a divorce May 18, according to documents obtained by Fox News Digital. A judge finalized the end to their marriage Friday.
JELLY ROLL, BUNNIE XO HINTED AT DIVORCE WEEKS BEFORE THE NEWS BROKE WITH CRYPTIC LYRICS AND MISSING RINGS
Jelly Roll has dodged rumors of infidelity as the cause of his divorce with Bunnie Xo. (Terry Wyatt/WireImage)
He listed the date of separation as May 9 and cited irreconcilable differences.
"Nobody cheated," Bailee said on the livestream, according to People. "Period. [Get] the f--- out of my comments, my DMs, my live with that s---, I don’t care, I don’t want to talk about it."

She told her followers they had "no f---ing idea what happened, and wait ‘til y’all find out," before threatening that "the internet in totality is about to f---ing crumble the day that I open my mouth."
BUNNIE XO SAYS SHE FUNDED JELLY ROLL'S EARLY CAREER BY 'TURNING TRICKS' WHILE REFLECTING ON DIVORCE
"It’s not a difference in f---ing opinions," she said. "Nobody else lived in it. So don’t f---ing even. I’m for real so done. Good? Everybody good? We’re on the same page? Cool."
Jelly Roll has two children from previous relationships. (Getty Images)
Bunnie Xo and Jelly Roll (born Jason DeFord) have fiercely defended their private relationship after news of their split broke the internet with accusations of cheating.
Terms of their settlement remain confidential. However, People reported the former couple will split their assets, including homes, cars, an aircraft and any intellectual property.
Additionally, the "Save Me" singer will make a "one-time, confidential lump sum payment to Bunnie, so there will be no alimony claims to be made in court," the outlet reported.

Of the many topics discussed in her since-scrubbed "divorce" podcast episode, Bunnie admitted her past life as a high-end escort funded their lifestyle when they first dated.

And, I mean, I had sugar daddies at the time that were paying for all of this."

title: LeAnn Rimes shares naked hot tub photo with Eddie Cibrian on road trip from California to Nashville
summary: LeAnn Rimes shared a naked hot tub photo with Eddie Cibrian during their cross-country road trip from California back to Nashville on Instagram.
story: The "Blue" singer said she and Cibrian love each other and can be stupid together.
LeAnn Rimes is spending her road trip from California back home to Nashville naked in a hot tub with her husband, Eddie Cibrian.

On Tuesday, Rimes took to Instagram to document their journey. In the carousel of images, the singer and actress shared a photo at the end of her post, taken from behind. Cibrian had his arm around her while she sat naked in the hot tub, taking in the scenic view.
"The last picture is what its ALL about. @leannrimes ❤️," one user commented, referencing the hot tub photo. Another added, "The last photo with you and @eddiecibrian just warms my heart!"
LeAnn Rimes and Eddie Cibrian cuddled in the hot tub in one image the singer shared to her Instagram page. (LeAnn Rimes/Instagram)

"there were questionable roadside sightings, car karaoke, a LOT of gas station potty breaks, incredible food and a few moments that probably should’ve stayed off camera… but didn’t."

Rimes and Cibrian enjoyed the hot tub on their road trip from California to Nashville. (Monica Schipper/Getty Images)

title: Ella Langley joins music royalty with 'insane' milestone for 'Choosin' Texas'
summary: Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas" tied a Billboard Hot 100 record with 14 weeks at No. 1, matching Mariah Carey and Whitney Houston among non-holiday titles by women.
story: Ella Langley discusses releasing a series of singles and building momentum toward her sophomore album while at the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards.
Ella Langley likely has a smile written on her face.
Her "Choosin' Texas" anthem placed at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 charts, its 14th week at the top, tying a record with two iconic hits.
Langley, 27, called the career milestone "insane" in a post shared on Instagram stories shortly after earning the spot.
ELLA LANGLEY SUFFERS WARDROBE MALFUNCTION WHILE OPENING FOR MORGAN WALLEN IN BALTIMORE
Ella Langley topped the Billboard Hot 100 charts for the 14th week in a row with her "Choosin' Texas" anthem. (John Schearer)

The country ballad first topped the Hot 100 in February and now matches Mariah Carey's "We Belong Together" and Whitney Houston's "I Will Always Love You" for most weeks at No. 1 among non-holiday titles by women with no male-billed acts.
In addition, "Choosing Texas" ties Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" for second-longest ranking hit.
Ella Langley celebrated her 14th week at the top of the Billboard 100 charts. (Instagram/Ella Langley)
Langley broke onto the country music scene nearly a decade ago and released her debut studio album, "Hungover," in 2024.
MORGAN WALLEN AND ELLA LANGLEY HOLD THE TOP TWO ALBUM SPOTS IN AMERICA FOR FIRST HALF OF 2026
The catalog brought her immediate accolades with hits, including "You Look Like You Love Me" and "Weren't for the Wind" both reaching No. 1 on country charts.
Her sophomore release, "Dandelion," debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 200 upon its release in April.
Ella Langley released her debut studio album in 2024. (Rich Polk/Billboard)
"Choosin' Texas" not only capped the Billboard Hot 100, but recently earned Langley the title of first female artist to simultaneously top the Hot 100, Hot Country Songs and Country Airplay charts.
MIRANDA LAMBERT DELIVERS STRAIGHT-SHOOTING ADVICE TO RISING COUNTRY STAR IN SURPRISE BATHROOM ENCOUNTER
The "Dandelion" title was inspired by the sturdy plant which is known to withstand challenging environments.

"I learned that dandelion tea is actually a natural detox for the liver," Ella told Billboard ahead of the release. "So, a record called ‘Dandelion’ after a record called hungover made all the sense in the world to me.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Ella Langley has become one of country music's fastest-rising stars. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I’ve never poured more of myself into a project, into a song, into an idea, and it’s fallen out so beautifully. It’s about learning yourself, making mistakes and realizing that it’s all just part of life.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I want this record to be something that fans can relate to but also something they want to get up and dance to at the same time. To me, this record feels like fireflies in the summertime. It feels like windows down on a red dirt road. It feels like the best kind of Sunday afternoon. It feels like those days I remember as a kid where it felt like there weren’t enough hours in the day. This record is really a love letter to that."
Langley served as executive producer on the album and co-wrote "Choosin' Texas" alongside Miranda Lambert, Luke Dick and JoyBeth Taylor.

title: Sharon Stone's terrifying weed withdrawal sparks warning about today's potent marijuana
summary: Sharon Stone's marijuana withdrawal symptoms were so severe that she saw a neurologist, highlighting the dangers of quitting high-potency THC without a plan.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses new research that casts doubt on cannabis benefits and highlights increased mental health risks, especially for teenagers. Modern marijuana, with 70-90% THC potency, is linked to higher rates of PTSD, anxiety, depression, ADHD, and bipolar disorder. Usage among Americans aged 12 and older has skyrocketed by 180% since the early 2000s, leading to concerns about addiction and health issues.
Hollywood icon Sharon Stone recently opened up about a health scare after quitting marijuana, revealing her symptoms were so intense that she turned to a neurologist.
During an interview with Variety, the actress said her decision to quit was driven by a desire for a drug-free life.
"And because I think they put so much stuff in it now — they really do — when I stopped smoking pot, I also got sick," she said.
CANNABIS COMPOUNDS COULD REVERSE DISEASE AFFECTING ONE-THIRD OF ADULTS
"I got pretty sick for a month. I went to my neurologist, and he said, ‘Sharon, I’ve had people dying in the emergency room from marijuana.'"
Stone attributed her ordeal to the potency of modern weed, saying, "It’s not like you’re pulling it out of the ground anymore ... It’s not like when we were kids."
American actress Sharon Stone quit "smoking pot" and got so sick that she consulted a neurologist, she revealed in a recent interview. (Getty Images, iStock)

Experts note that cannabis withdrawal itself is generally not considered life-threatening, although severe symptoms, underlying medical conditions or interactions with other substances can complicate recovery.
FLYING WITH CANNABIS? TSA'S NEW GUIDANCE COMES WITH A MAJOR HEALTH WARNING
Dr. Chris Tuell, clinical director of addiction services at the Lindner Center in Cincinnati, confirmed that today's cannabis products are vastly different from the strains of decades past.
THC levels in marijuana have surged from about 3% to 5% in the 1980s to as high as 30% in today's cannabis products, while concentrates can exceed 90% THC, he told Fox News Digital.
"I do believe cannabis is addicting, especially with the high levels of THC."

Higher THC concentrations have been linked to greater risks of dependence, cannabis use disorder (CUD), psychosis in some users and more severe withdrawal symptoms, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse.

As today's cannabis products become increasingly potent, experts say there are several risks and warning signs that daily users should know before deciding whether to continue — or quit — using marijuana.
No. 1: High-potency THC changes the brain's reward system
According to Cleveland Clinic, CUD occurs when marijuana takes over the brain's reward pathways, amplifying compulsive behavior.
"I do believe cannabis is addicting, especially with the high levels of THC," Tuell told Fox News Digital.
No. 2: Addiction isn't always obvious

The American Psychiatric Association’s DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition) outlines the following diagnostic criteria signaling that casual use may have crossed into dependency.

Today’s cannabis flower and concentrates contain up to 90% THC, making modern products exponentially stronger than those from decades past, experts say. (iStock)
No. 3: Withdrawal can be intense
Quitting heavy, long-term cannabis use can trigger withdrawal symptoms within 24 to 48 hours, Cleveland Clinic notes.

Users frequently experience severe insomnia, intense irritability, anxiety, appetite loss, sweating, headaches and stomach upset. While acute physical symptoms typically resolve within a month, mood swings and sleep issues can linger much longer, according to Tuell.

4. Medical guidance may be needed

While cannabis withdrawal alone rarely requires hospitalization, Cleveland Clinic notes that people with significant medical or mental health conditions — or those stopping cannabis while also withdrawing from alcohol, opioids or certain other medications — may benefit from medical supervision.
Addiction experts strongly advise stepping down THC intake slowly to cushion the impact on the nervous system and avoid severe rebound symptoms. (iStock)
No. 5: Underlying issues may fuel dependence

Mental health conditions often occur alongside cannabis use disorder, and treating those underlying issues may help reduce problematic marijuana use, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Cleveland Clinic.

"I strongly believe that CUD and mental health issues co-exist, and that mental health counseling can address the issues driving the addictive behaviors," Tuell said.

title: Microplastics detected in most heart attack patients' blood in startling new study
summary: Nearly 84% of severe heart attack patients had detectable microplastics in their coronary artery blood, with polyethylene found in 97% of cases.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel sits down with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin for an exclusive interview on a new push to remove microplastics from the food supply and environment.

Patients experiencing severe heart attacks may have significantly higher concentrations of micro- and nanoplastics in their blood compared to individuals with stable heart conditions, according to new research.
Italian researchers analyzed blood samples from the coronary arteries of 61 patients undergoing angiograms, a procedure that analyzes blood vessels for irregularities.

They found that nearly 84% of patients suffering an active, severe heart attack had detectable micro- and nanoplastics in their blood. In contrast, plastic was detected in 40% of patients with chronic heart disease and only 32% of those with normal coronary arteries.
NOTABLE FIGURES WHO DIED FROM THE SAME HEART CONDITION LINKED TO LINDSEY GRAHAM'S DEATH
Researchers led by Dr. Raffaele Marfella of the University of Campania Luigi Vanvitelli in Naples conducted the study, which was published in the European Heart Journal.
Polyethylene, a common material used in plastic bags and bottles, appeared in 97% of those patients who tested positive.
Severe heart attack patients were significantly more likely to have micro- and nanoplastics in their blood than those with stable heart conditions or clear arteries. (iStock)

"This study adds to emerging research showing the potential role of micro- and nanoplastics in heart disease," Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished.com, told Fox News Digital.
While notable, the findings should be considered in the broader context of environmental health hazards, said New York City-based Routhenstein, who was not involved in the study.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

"While these findings are interesting and highlight the importance of paying attention to environmental factors that may contribute to inflammation and blood vessel injury, they do not prove that plastics cause heart attacks," she said.
The findings align with previous research detecting microplastics in arterial plaque, Routhenstein noted, although she cautioned that the study has several limitations.
A history of smoking emerged as the single strongest predictor of detectable plastic particles in the blood, the researchers found. (iStock)

"This was an observational study, so it can only show an association, not cause and effect," she said. "It also included a relatively small group of patients from one country, so we can't assume the findings apply to everyone."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Health and environmental variables could also complicate the data. In the study, a history of smoking emerged as the single strongest predictor of detectable plastic particles in the blood.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Factors like smoking and air pollution are also linked to cardiovascular disease and higher plastic exposure, making it difficult to separate the independent effects of microplastics," Routhenstein said.
Heating food in glass or ceramic instead of plastic is one way to reduce exposure to microplastics, according to experts. (iStock)
To reduce potential risk, the dietitian recommends making targeted swaps to help limit daily exposure to microplastics.

"I would take inventory of your regular sources of microplastic exposure and see where you can reduce or swap them for better alternatives," Routhenstein said. "For example, replace plastic food storage containers with glass ones."
She also urged taking extra precautions when preparing meals and drinking water.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"When microwaving or reheating food, use glass or ceramic containers instead of plastic," she said. "It's also a good idea to limit plastic water bottles and single-use plastic containers, especially when they're exposed to heat."
She added, "Think of reducing plastic exposure as one piece of an overall heart-healthy lifestyle."

title: Men switched at birth uncover hospital mix-up after DNA test decades later
summary: A DNA test gift revealed Kyle Bylin had no genetic match to his family, leading to the discovery he and Jeremy Morrison were switched at birth in 1988.
story: Jeremy Morrison and Kyle Bylin, born in 1988, share their story after a DNA test revealed they were switched at birth nearly 40 years ago. The men are now suing Unity Medical Center in North Dakota for answers, as the hospital claims no existing records from that time. This extraordinary case highlights the emotional impact of such a mix-up.

Two North Dakota men are suing a local hospital after discovering they were switched at birth nearly four decades ago, a revelation brought to light by a surprise result from a direct-to-consumer genetic test.
The men joined Fox & Friends on Thursday to discuss their journey.

The mix-up was uncovered two years ago when Kyle Bylin received an at-home DNA test as a gift. Bylin says he was shocked when the results showed no genetic match to anyone in the family that raised him.
TWO FAMILIES SUE NORTH DAKOTA HOSPITAL ON ALLEGATIONS BABIES WERE SWITCHED AT BIRTH
"It was absolutely mind-blowing," Bylin told Fox & Friends. "We knew the DNA trail didn’t make sense, but to find out you’ve been switched at birth is a huge revelation."

Instead, the data pointed to a biological aunt, leading Bylin to her nephew, Jeremy Morrison. Subsequent DNA testing confirmed that Morrison and Bylin had been raised by each other’s biological families.
"[My parents] will always be my parents. A DNA test isn’t going to change 38 years of memories overnight," Morrison said.
Kyle Bylin and Jeremy Morrison were the only two babies born at Unity Medical Center in Grafton, North Dakota, on Jan. 26, 1988, the lawsuit says. (Google Maps)
Morrison recalled having long-standing doubts while growing up, noting that he often made light of the physical differences between himself and the woman who raised him.
MELINDA FRENCH GATES SAYS IT TOOK 3 DOCTORS TO DIAGNOSE THE CONDITION SHE WAS SUFFERING FROM
"I kind of had a feeling inside that I was adopted or, you know, she stole me or something like that," Morrison said. But that doesn’t necessarily mean he’d change what happened, he added.
"It’s a little bit of nature, a little bit of nurture, and you end up with the life that you have," he said when asked if he’d go back and undo the switch.
SISTERS IN VIRAL VIDEO REVEAL TRUTH OF 'EERIE' FAMILY PHOTO THEY DISCOVERED AT RENTAL HOME
The emotional toll of the discovery has weighed heavily on both men as they grapple with the realization that their upbringings were altered.
The hospital has denied the men's allegations. (Getty Images)
"Do I feel like I lost the ability to truly connect with my biological parents? Absolutely," Bylin said.

The two men filed a lawsuit against Unity Medical Center alleging emotional distress caused by negligence and medical malpractice, claiming the facility robbed them of the lives they were meant to live.

Unity Medical Center denied responsibility for the incident, asserting that an internal review yielded no evidence showing hospital personnel were at fault. However, the medical center did not dispute that the swap occurred.

"We recognize the profound impact this discovery has had on them and their families," the hospital said in a statement.
The men said they knew that the DNA trail didn’t make sense, but that finding out they’ve been switched at birth was a huge revelation. (iStock)
"While we deeply sympathize with the men and their families, we have found no evidence to support claims that Unity Medical Center or its staff were responsible for what occurred."

Although both Bylin and Morrison have since met their respective biological parents, the two men have yet to meet each other in person.
"It’s a little bit of nature, a little bit of nurture, and you end up with the life that you have."

"There are no plans in the works right now," Morrison said. "I grew up with his entire family. And he grew up with my entire family," he added, as the reason the two men "don’t feel like" they need to meet.

Despite the legal battle and the lingering disruption to their lives, both men said they are focusing on moving forward and making the best of their circumstances.
"We’re just trying to raise awareness of this situation," Bylin added.

title: FDA to review 7 popular peptides touted for weight loss, healing and longevity
summary: The FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee weighs peptides for obesity, insulin resistance, opioid withdrawal and insomnia this week.
story: Dr. Alex Tatem, a board-certified urologist in Indiana, discusses why upcoming federal hearings on seven peptides were mandated and argues that years of patient use show a promising safety profile.
The Food and Drug Administration is taking a closer look this week at seven unapproved peptide substances that have surged in popularity for their purported health benefits.

At meetings scheduled for July 23 and 24 at the FDA’s White Oak Campus in Silver Spring, Maryland, the FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee will consider whether to recommend adding seven peptide substances to the agency’s 503A Bulks List, which would allow them to be used in certain compounded prescription drugs.
Although these peptides are not FDA-approved, they are widely available through wellness clinics, compounding operations and gray-market online sellers.
THINKING ABOUT PEPTIDES? DOCTORS REVEAL KEY DOS AND DONT'S AS 'WILD WEST' MARKET GROWS

HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has voiced support for expanding access to certain peptide therapies, while FDA reviewers have raised concerns about the limited evidence supporting the safety and effectiveness of the seven substances under consideration.

According to Reuters, consumer demand is likely to "remain strong" despite the outcome, as peptides have surged in popularity for weight loss, muscle building, performance enhancement, chronic disease management and even wound repair.
Peptides have surged in popularity for weight loss, muscle building, performance enhancement, chronic disease management and even wound repair. (iStock)

Proposed use: Ulcerative colitis

Proposed use: Wound healing
Proposed forms: Subcutaneous or intramuscular injection

Proposed forms: Cream and gel

Proposed use: Obesity and osteoporosis
Proposed forms: Subcutaneous injection

No. 6: Emideltide
Proposed use: Opioid withdrawal, chronic insomnia, narcolepsy
Proposed form: Subcutaneous injection

Proposed use: Insomnia
Proposed form: Subcutaneous injection
"These were all medications that were designed to help people live well and live as healthy as possible," Tatem previously told Fox News Digital about peptides. (iStock)
Performance potential
Performance medicine and peptide expert Dr. Alex Tatem, a board-certified urologist and member of Rugiet's Medical Advisory Board, will testify at this week's FDA hearings.
In an interview with Fox News Digital, Indiana-based Tatem said that every product up for review is "exciting," as each targets a different problem faced by patients.

"BPC-157 or TB-500 are compounds that can help facilitate healing after injury and have been shown in multiple studies to be incredibly safe when administered — which is interesting when you compare that to the over-the-counter options that we use now for aches and pains, like ibuprofen," he said.

Although ibuprofen is available over the counter, the FDA warns that it can cause serious side effects — including stomach bleeding, kidney damage and cardiovascular complications — especially when used at high doses or for long periods.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Tatem claimed that millions of BPC-157 doses have been administered and that relatively few adverse events have been reported.

"There is no other drug on the market that had that sort of safety record," Tatem said. "And it's not because of any magic — it's because these are natural substances that our bodies make and are familiar with, so that's what gives them this incredible safety profile."
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. testifies during the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health hearing on June 24, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc)

The FDA, however, has publicly stated that there is not enough evidence from human clinical trials on the safety or efficacy of these drugs. FDA reviewers have also cautioned that a peptide’s similarity to a naturally occurring substance does not eliminate potential risks.
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel cautioned that these substances "need careful study."
"I am not convinced the data is fully there yet."
According to the doctor, RFK Jr. told Siegel in their latest interview that he believes "not all peptides are created equal, whereas some are helpful, others may not be and need further study."

"I agree with that," Siegel told Fox News Digital. "I’m concerned about the impact some may have on the kidneys. I would like to see rigorous clinical trials before approval. I am not convinced the data is fully there yet."
Next steps

Tatem said he expects the hearings to be a "hard-fought battle," but hopes committee members will consider what he described as real-world data from tens of millions of doses administered between 2014 and 2023. The data showed adverse event rates of "well under 0.1%," he added.
If the committee recommends inclusion, the FDA would still need to complete its review and rulemaking process before formally adding any of the substances to the 503A Bulks List.

That list includes active ingredients that state-licensed pharmacies are legally permitted to use for compounding prescription drugs, Tatem said.

He also suggested that the FDA could place some substances under a more permissive enforcement category temporarily while the rulemaking process continues. (The agency has not announced that it intends to do so.)

"Ultimately, what we would hope is, before the end of the year, patients would be able to go to their doctor, work through maybe a telehealth provider, and then be able to get a prescription for this under monitored medical supervision," he said.
"The most important thing to take away is that your voice matters."

"The most important thing to take away is that your voice matters, because this committee is just issuing a recommendation to the FDA. The FDA can take it or leave it," Tatem noted. "Everything that happens afterward is still anyone's guess."

title: CDC reveals massive behind-the-scenes public health operation that kept FIFA World Cup fans safe
summary: The CDC operated behind the scenes during the FIFA World Cup, deploying disease surveillance, wastewater monitoring and real-time data dashboards.
story: Andrew Giuliani outlines the significant economic and security preparations for the 2026 FIFA World Cup. He reveals 78 matches will occur across 11 cities, projecting a $30.5 billion boost to the American economy.

FIRST ON FOX: The World Cup tested not only the players on the pitch, but the Trump administration's large public health operation to safeguard the public as fans from all over the world moved across the United States.

Amid the fandom, as 11 American cities hosted 39 teams and 78 matches, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) operated largely behind the scenes to detect emerging threats and to respond to public health emergencies.
"Readiness is not only measured by how we respond to emergencies, but by the work we do every day to prevent them," acting CDC Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya said in a statement to Fox News Digital.
"The FIFA World Cup demonstrated the strength of CDC’s partnerships, preparedness and commitment to protecting the health of every community we serve."
CONGO TEAM MUST ISOLATE TO ENTER UNITED STATES FOR WORLD CUP AMID EBOLA OUTBREAK

Fans gather before the FIFA World Cup 2026 final match between Spain and Argentina at New Jersey Stadium, also known as MetLife Stadium, in East Rutherford, N.J., July 19, 2026. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tracked public health threats behind the scenes during the tournament. (Anadolu via Getty Images)
In total, the FIFA World Cup hosted 48 teams across 16 cities in the U.S., Canada and Mexico, with more than 5 million tickets sold.

An estimated 6.5 million fans from around the world converged in the three host countries, bringing their passion, enthusiasm and, possibly, germs. Overlapping with Independence Day celebrations, large gatherings were common, as well as the backdrop of concurrent international disease activity, including the Ebola and Hantavirus outbreaks.
Infectious disease can easily spread in large crowds, and experts were already looking at wastewater, a possible uptick in hospital visits and social media for any signs of a potential outbreak.
Diseases like measles are always a top concern. As of July 16, there were 2,260 confirmed measles cases in the U.S., according to the CDC.
"The matches drew the world's attention. The work that kept them healthy did not — and that was the point," the CDC said in a news release Sunday.
FBI BOSS KASH PATEL DETAILS HOW AGENCY AND PARTNERS SECURED RECORD-SHATTERING FIFA WORLD CUP
MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J., hosted games during the 2026 World Cup. (Getty Images)

The CDC's effort included a World Cup data dashboard that provided health departments with real-time data on disease trends across multiple cities as fans and teams traveled throughout the tournament, as well as around-the-clock health operations at U.S. ports of entry in coordination with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to monitor international passengers.
The agency also deployed its experts to strengthen disease surveillance, laboratory capacity, wastewater surveillance and preparedness planning in host cities.

In all, the agency coordinated across a broad network, including multiple CDC divisions, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response (ASPR) and the White House FIFA World Cup Task Force.
WHITE HOUSE ADDRESSES GROWING PARASITE OUTBREAK AFTER MORE THAN 400 AMERICANS SICKENED

In March, the CDC released guidance providing health officials with a framework for preparing for a broad range of threats, including biological, chemical, radiologic/nuclear, environmental and mass casualty incidents.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) headquarters in Atlanta. (AP Photo/Jeff Amy, File)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The guidance encouraged every jurisdiction to approach the tournament through a risk-based lens, recognizing that travel between venues connects communities far beyond the host cities.

The tournament is over, but the work is not. The same preparedness, surveillance and partnerships that supported the World Cup are part of CDC's readiness and response mission every day of the year, continuing through the close of the activation on July 31 and well beyond.

title: Experts reveal how to avoid deadly Legionnaires' disease as NYC outbreak kills 5
summary: The New York City Legionnaires' disease outbreak has killed five and sickened 82, but doctors say key prevention steps can reduce exposure risk.
story: NYC health officials warn residents of a Legionnaires' disease outbreak with 23 confirmed cases. Dr. Stephanie Widmer explains the bacterial pneumonia, its symptoms like cough and fever and its curability.

As New York City continues to investigate an outbreak of Legionnaires' disease that has claimed multiple lives and sickened dozens of people, doctors say there are ways people can reduce the risk of exposure.

As of July 21, there have been five deaths and 82 diagnoses linked to the Upper East Side outbreak, according to the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene. Eight patients remain hospitalized.
Health officials said no new cases had been reported in the previous six days, suggesting the source of exposure has likely been eliminated, although the investigation remains ongoing.
NYC LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE OUTBREAK KILLS FOURTH VICTIM; 76 CASES REPORTED
Legionnaires’ disease is a serious type of pneumonia that is typically spread by tiny water droplets containing Legionella bacteria, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

As New York City continues to investigate an outbreak of Legionnaires' disease that has claimed multiple lives and sickened dozens of people, doctors say there are ways people can reduce the risk of exposure. (iStock)
Sources of exposure

Common sources of infection include contaminated building water systems, such as cooling towers (large structures that remove heat from water used in building cooling systems), hot tubs or plumbing. Cases have also been reported on cruise ships and in spas. It is not generally spread from person to person, according to the CDC.

"We get infected when it gets aerosolized in the water droplets, usually, and we breathe those droplets in," Dr. Dana Mordue, associate professor of pathology, microbiology and immunology at New York Medical College, told Fox News Digital.
NYC HEALTH OFFICIALS WARN CENTRAL PARK VISITORS AFTER LEGIONNAIRES’ OUTBREAK GROWS ON UPPER EAST SIDE

"You can also get infected if you have water that's been contaminated, and you aspirate it and swallow it into your lungs, but most often you get it from air droplets that are contaminated from various types of water sources."
Legionnaires’ disease is a serious type of pneumonia that is typically spread by tiny water droplets containing Legionella bacteria. (iStock)

Although it is possible to contract Legionnaires’ in the home, outbreaks are almost always linked to exposure to water droplets coming from a water system in a "commercial-type building," according to Mordue.

"The good news is you usually don't get it from the types of cooling systems that we have in our cars or our homes. But if you don't clean your humidifiers, technically any water source can get contaminated with Legionella."
Symptoms and treatment

The most widespread symptoms of Legionnaires' disease include cough, shortness of breath, fever, muscle aches and headaches, according to the CDC. Some people may also experience diarrhea, nausea and confusion.
Symptoms typically begin two to 14 days after exposure to the bacteria, although they can appear later. The illness often requires treatment with antibiotics.
The most widespread symptoms of Legionnaires' disease include cough, shortness of breath, fever, muscle aches and headaches, according to the CDC.  (iStock)
"The mortality rate is not particularly high for this disease if you are immune-competent and young and healthy," said Mordue.
Risk is higher for older adults, smokers and people with compromised immune systems, "a lot of the same risk factors you might see for COVID," the doctor noted.
Ways to prevent spread
The CDC shares the following measures to prevent the spread of Legionnaires’ disease.

Maintain building water systems. Comprehensive water management programs can prevent Legionella bacteria from growing in cooling towers, plumbing systems, hot tubs and other building water systems. The CDC estimates that nearly nine in 10 outbreaks could have been prevented with more effective water management.Clean and disinfect cooling towers. These structures should be routinely cleaned, monitored and disinfected to control bacteria growth, health officials recommend.Prevent stagnant water. Maintaining proper water flow and flushing any pipes that are infrequently used can help prevent Legionella from multiplying.Maintain proper water temperature and disinfectant levels. As Legionella is known to grow best in warm water (about 77°F to 113°F), maintaining appropriate temperatures and adequate disinfectant levels helps limit bacterial growth, the CDC says.

The CDC estimates that nearly nine in 10 outbreaks could have been prevented with more effective water management.
Clean and disinfect cooling towers. These structures should be routinely cleaned, monitored and disinfected to control bacteria growth, health officials recommend.
Prevent stagnant water. Maintaining proper water flow and flushing any pipes that are infrequently used can help prevent Legionella from multiplying.

Maintain proper water temperature and disinfectant levels. As Legionella is known to grow best in warm water (about 77°F to 113°F), maintaining appropriate temperatures and adequate disinfectant levels helps limit bacterial growth, the CDC says.

For anyone who may have been exposed and developed symptoms, it is important to seek immediate medical care, doctors say. Early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment can reduce the risk of severe illness.
"If you have certain risk factors, particularly advanced age, get help as quickly as you can," Mordue advised.

title: Pancreatic cancer vaccine shows promise in first human trial, preventing disease in high-risk patients
summary: A Johns Hopkins pancreatic cancer vaccine triggered immune responses in 90% of high-risk participants, with some cysts shrinking after vaccination.
story: Fox News senior correspondent Jonathan Serrie reports on doctors seeing results from Daraxonrasib, a new drug targeting pancreatic cancer, on ‘Special Report.’
A new vaccine for the prevention of pancreatic cancer has shown promise in an early study at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine in Baltimore, Maryland.
A phase 1 trial published in Cancer Discovery, a journal of the American Association for Cancer Research, tested an experimental vaccine called mKRAS-VAX in 20 people, according to a press release.

Participants had an inherited risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the most common and aggressive form of pancreatic cancer, along with an abnormality detected in imaging, typically a pancreatic cyst. These individuals had not been diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.
NEW PANCREATIC CANCER PILL NEARLY DOUBLES SURVIVAL TIME IN BREAKTHROUGH TRIAL
Four injections were administered to participants during weeks one, three and five, along with a booster at week 13.
The vaccine targeted six common mutations of KRAS. Changes in this gene drive more than 90% of PDACs.
The vaccine targeted six common mutations of KRAS. Changes in this gene drive more than 90% of PDACs. (iStock)

The vaccine triggered a mutant KRAS-targeted immune response in 18 of the 20 participants (90%). On average, immune activity increased about 18-fold, although responses varied. Half of participants responded to all six KRAS mutations included in the vaccine.
Researchers also found the vaccine generated two types of T cells — one to attack abnormal cells and another to provide longer-term immune memory.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The vaccine appeared to be safe, with participants experiencing only injection-site reactions and temporary flu-like symptoms.

While the phase 1 trial was designed primarily to evaluate safety rather than effectiveness, after about 16.5 months of follow-up, no participants had developed pancreatic cancer. At the same time, 37.5% of vaccinated participants experienced shrinkage or disappearance of the pancreatic cysts that had put them at increased risk for the disease.
Some pancreatic cancer cysts shrank or disappeared in vaccinated individuals, according to a press release. (iStock)

Study co-author Neeha Zaidi, MD, associate professor of oncology at the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center at Johns Hopkins University, commented that the long-lasting response of this vaccine is "particularly noteworthy when assessing for possible interception of cancer, which requires long-lasting immunity."

"In addition, the vaccine was safe and well-tolerated, supporting its use in larger cancer interception studies," she said in the press release. "Overall, this study represents the first proof of concept for the use of vaccines for interception of pancreatic cancer in human patients."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Co-author Michael G. Goggins, MD, professor of pathology, medicine and oncology and the Sol Goldman Professor of Pancreatic Cancer Research at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, also commented on the findings.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We observed evidence of stability or regression of the pancreatic cysts in association with the induction and durability of KRAS-specific T-cell responses," he said in the release. "However, larger studies are needed to demonstrate that this effect was in fact due to the vaccine."
The authors noted the study was limited by its small sample size and because it was not designed to determine clinical efficacy.
Prevention and interception "save lives and reduce the morbidity associated with cancer development and progression," a co-author says. (iStock)

Fellow senior author Elizabeth Jaffee, MD, deputy director of the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center at Johns Hopkins, commented that prevention and interception "save lives and reduce the morbidity associated with cancer development and progression."
"This is especially important for cancers whose early-onset frequency is increasing and for which we do not have effective methods for early detection," she added in the release.

Jaffee noted that this research highlights the need for more funding to support developing strategies for preventing cancer in high-risk individuals.
"More studies are needed to find the best vaccine approaches, the best targets and the ideal timing for vaccination," she said.

title: Michelin-star chef reveals what's replacing hospital food Americans love to hate
summary: Chef Geoffrey Zakarian reveals how he overhauled Tampa General Hospital's menu on a budget while eliminating seed oils and sugar and improving patient health.
story: After three years of rethinking hospital meals, Michelin star chef Geoffrey Zakarian is swapping boxed shakes, seed oils and sugar for fresh comfort food, smoothies and protein-rich dishes built around the idea that food can help with healing.
"Hospital food" has long been synonymous with packaged, ultraprocessed meals — despite the fact that hospitals are meant to promote healing.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital at the Great American State Fair in Washington, D.C., Michelin-star chef Geoffrey Zakarian shared his initiative to improve what is served in U.S. hospitals, following the concept that "food is medicine."
For the last three years, Zakarian said he’s been working on changing hospital food — most notably at Tampa General, which is a $4 billion nonprofit, 1,000-bed public hospital.
RFK HAILS FIRST US HOSPITAL TO PROMISE HEALTHIER MEALS: 'WE HAVE A TEMPLATE'

On Thursday, July 16, Tampa General Hospital CEO John Couris signed the "Make Hospital Food Healthier" pledge during a news conference attended by Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Secretary Brooke Rollins and Zakarian.
Michelin-star chef Geoffrey Zakarian sat down with Fox News Digital at the Great American State Fair in Washington, D.C., on July 6, 2026. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
The pledge commits the hospital to serving more nutritious, minimally processed meals to patients, building on Zakarian's menu overhaul.
"We’ve changed the entire menu," the celebrity chef told Fox News Digital. "We've taken all seed oils out, sugar, maltodextrin. Anything bad in a box is gone. Anything good is brought in."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We're serving mac and cheese. We're serving hanger steak and fries. We're serving chicken with couscous. We do all our protein shakes. No protein shakes in the box anymore. We do fruit shakes, smoothies, fresh sorbet," the chef listed. "So, you're eating like your grandmother's cooking for you."
CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz has also supported Zakarian in this mission, telling Fox News Digital that the chef has "revolutionized our thinking" around hospital food.

Michelin-star chef Geoffrey Zakarian and CMS Administrator Dr. Oz spoke with Fox News Digital at the Great American State Fair in Washington, D.C., on July 6, 2026. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)

"How do we get the hospitals to do what [Zakarian] has been doing the frontier work on, get them to actually embrace food as part of the healing process?" he questioned. "Because most patients, and most doctors, know that the food in the hospital is not going to make you better."
Oz noted that while hospital food may provide some nutrients, it is generally not seen as contributing meaningfully to patients' recovery.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The biggest challenge to getting better food into hospital systems has been cost, Zakarian pointed out.
While "everything is fractionalized," what’s left over after paying for supplies is put toward food, which generally "ain’t much," he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"It's, like, $3.50 a person per plate, which is an extraordinarily small amount," the chef said. "You go to McDonald's, and you spend 12 bucks for a happy meal, and we give you $3.50 in a hospital. So that's an unhappy meal as far as I'm concerned."
Instead of charging hospitals for each plate served, Zakarian's approach relies on a flat annual fee, saving money through a smaller, higher-quality menu.
Tampa General Hospital (not pictured) worked with a chef to revamp its menu and make it more nutritious. (iStock)
"Yummy food, not just food to fill people up," he said. "Nutritious food, bioavailable food, food that's satiating."
"I'm cooking like I would cook in a restaurant. I'm cooking like my mother cooked for me. There's no difference."

The chef continued, "When you're lying in bed in a hospital gown, you feel alone, you feel exposed, you feel sick … When you have a fresh protein shake or a fresh healthy smoothie, or you can order steak frites ... that [makes] your day."
Freelance writer Teresa Mull contributed to this report.

title: Melinda French Gates says it took 3 doctors to diagnose the condition she was suffering from
summary: Melinda French Gates says it took three doctors to diagnose her perimenopause, revealing a startling gap in OB-GYN menopause training nationwide.
story: Dr. Amy Wechsler, a dual board-certified dermatologist and psychiatrist in Manhattan, reveals how she helps women who are battling acne as they age.
Melinda French Gates is speaking out about the challenges of recognizing perimenopause, saying she didn't receive the proper diagnosis and treatment until after seeing three different doctors.
She shared her experience with journalist Norah O'Donnell's new podcast "Healthful," which will be released on Wednesday.
French Gates, now 61, said she was in her early 40s when she began experiencing menopause symptoms, noting that she "kind of couldn't believe it," as reported by CBS News.
LOW TESTOSTERONE? HEGSETH SPARKS CONVERSATION AS DOCTORS REVEAL WARNING SIGNS EVERY MAN SHOULD KNOW
Later, the philanthropist and businesswoman would learn that many OB-GYNs receive little formal training in menopause care, which she says underscores a broader gap in women's healthcare.

Melinda French Gates is speaking out about the challenges of recognizing perimenopause, saying she didn't receive the proper diagnosis and treatment until after seeing three different doctors. (Getty Images)

"But it was kind of unbelievable to me that, even in this, you know, unbelievably privileged situation I'm in, where I feel like I can get some of the best healthcare, it took me three doctors to really diagnose what I was going through and to get the right treatments for where I was," she said during the interview.

"It wasn't because anybody was doing the wrong thing. It's because of what I now know, which is, only one-third of OB-GYNs in this country are trained in menopause."

Supporting her claim, a national survey published in the journal Menopause in 2023 found that only about one-third of U.S. obstetrics and gynecology residency programs include a formal menopause curriculum.

"It wasn't because anybody was doing the wrong thing. It's because of what I now know, which is, only one-third of OB-GYNs in this country are trained in menopause," French Gates told journalist Norah O'Donnell on her podcast "Healthful." (Getty Images)

In a separate 2026 Kansas study, more than half of residents reported receiving fewer than five hours of menopause education — and the majority did not believe that residency fully prepared them to treat menopausal patients independently.

Some of the most common include irregular periods, hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disturbances, mood changes, vaginal dryness, brain fog and joint pain as hormone levels begin to fluctuate, according to Mayo Clinic.

title: NYC Legionnaires' disease outbreak kills fourth victim, 76 cases reported
summary: A fourth person has died as 76 Legionnaires' disease cases are now linked to cooling towers in Upper East Side buildings, including the Guggenheim Museum.

An outbreak of Legionnaires' disease in New York City killed a fourth person as 76 cases have now been reported in the city, city health authorities announced Monday.

The outbreak, which city authorities have linked to a series of cooling towers in Upper East Side buildings, has hospitalized 60 people, 53 of whom were discharged while seven remained in the hospital, according to authorities.
The fourth death announced Monday follows a first death from the disease on Friday. City officials announced two additional deaths over the weekend.
DEADLY LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE OUTBREAK SPARKS CONCERN IN MAJOR US CITY: KNOW THE SYMPTOMS
