title: Six-figure private security bill for top Dem Senate hopeful fuels GOP hypocrisy claims
summary: Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper spent more than a quarter-million dollars this election cycle on private security, leading to calls of hypocrisy from critics citing his "soft-on-crime" record.
story: Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., announced he and his wife, Teresa, have sold the McDonald's restaurant business they spent decades building, allowing him to dedicate more of his time to representing western North Carolina in Congress.

FIRST ON FOX: Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper’s Senate campaign spent more than $250,000 on private security, federal records reviewed by Fox News Digital show, giving Republicans a new line of attack as they accuse the Democratic Senate hopeful of backing policies that make North Carolinians feel less safe.

Federal Election Commission records show Cooper’s campaign spent $277,312 on security-related payments during the 2026 election cycle thus far, with the money going to two vendors — Foresight Solutions and Frontpoint.

Foresight Solutions describes its work as including customized security assessments, workplace safety training, de-escalation techniques, conflict resolution and workplace violence prevention. Frontpoint markets home-security systems designed to protect homes and families.
SUPREME COURT JUSTICES MAKE RARE CAPITOL HILL APPEARANCE TO PUSH $230M SECURITY BUDGET

The spending comes as Cooper faces GOP attacks over his record on policing, criminal justice reform, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) cooperation and COVID-19-era inmate releases during his time as governor.

Republicans also have invoked the killing of Ukrainian refugee Iryna Zarutska on a Charlotte light rail train, arguing Cooper’s criminal justice posture — including a racial equity task force that backed changes to cash bail — reflects a broader soft-on-crime record.

Republican strategist Mark Bednar, who was a communications director for former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy and current Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, ripped Cooper's "blatant hypocrisy" in a statement to Fox News Digital.
Fox News Digital obtained this image of Roy Cooper in Durham, N.C., as he headed to a campaign rally April 9, 2026, with armed security by his side. (Obtained by Fox News Digital)

"The issue on voters' minds isn't whether Roy Cooper or any other Democrat deems it necessary to keep themselves safe, but the issue is when he and other Democrats prioritize their own security while trying to hide from voters' their soft-on-crime records that threaten local communities," Bednar said.

"As Governor, Roy Cooper agreed to release thousands of criminals early, many of whom went on to commit more crimes, and he fought tooth and nail to prevent local law enforcement working with immigration enforcement officials," he continued. "In an election year that's going to come down to the wire, blatant hypocrisy like this is going to stick out to voters."

However, a Cooper campaign spokesperson pushed back on the criticism, defending the former governor's public safety record and accusing his Republican opponent in the upcoming general election, Michael Whatley, of hypocrisy.
WHATLEY LINKS COOPER TO TRANSIT KILLING, ACCUSES DEM OF FREEING ‘RAPISTS AND MURDERERS’

A massive spike in applications to North Carolina’s school voucher program means most higher-income families won’t receive financial help for the coming year even though the General Assembly did away with income caps on the program.  (Getty Images )

"While Roy spent his career putting rapists and violent criminals behind bars and signing tough-on-crime, stricter bail and pretrial release laws as governor, Michael Whatley spent his (career) appointing a convicted child sex predator who served time in prison to a powerful position within the North Carolina Republican Party and pushing to release prisoners during the pandemic," the spokesperson said, referring to Whatley's appointment of Harvey Lee West.

West pleaded guilty in 2000 to five counts of taking indecent liberties with a child and later served on the North Carolina GOP’s Plan of Organization Committee, which helps set party rules, according to PolitiFact.

The Cooper campaign suggested Republicans have been distorting Cooper’s record on COVID-era inmate releases, pointing to past statements from the North Carolina GOP under Whatley that criticized Cooper for not doing more to address COVID-19 inside prisons.

Cooper’s campaign also pointed to the former governor's 16 years as North Carolina attorney general and legislation he signed as governor that made it easier to go after drug dealers, gave judges discretion to keep violent offenders behind bars ahead of trial and provided raises to law enforcement.
Republican Michael Whatley and Democrat Roy Cooper   (Angela Weiss/AFP/Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
A Whatley spokesperson clapped back at Cooper's claims when asked for a response, arguing the former governor has a long record of mismanaging significant challenges.

"Roy Cooper has blood on his hands. He chose to release thousands of convicted criminals back onto North Carolina’s streets instead of fighting in court like Democrat governors in Colorado and Illinois," Whatley spokesperson DJ Griffin told Fox News Digital in response to Cooper's criticism.
"The consequences have been devastating."
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Defense industry leaders align with Trump admin plans in closed-door strategy session on defense spending
summary: Susie Wiles and leaders from Raytheon, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman and Palantir aligned on $73 billion in Pentagon and intelligence funding.
story: Fox News' Steve Harrigan reports on Kuwait confronting Iranian missiles and drones on 'The Story.'

EXCLUSIVE: High-level Trump administration officials, including chief of staff Susie Wiles, met Thursday morning at the White House with key defense industry stakeholders, and White House officials laid out their vision for the House of Representatives' current budget reconciliation package related to crucial funding for the Iran war.

Wiles, Department of War and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) leaders and leaders from 17 top defense contractors including Raytheon, BAE Systems, Honeywell, Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, Palantir and others, were in attendance for the meeting, according to a Trump administration official.
The Trump administration representatives laid out their vision for what is being called "Reconciliation 3.0."
The purpose of the meeting was to ensure that all the companies were aligned on the importance of this reconciliation package being passed, which, according to the administration official, they were.
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOUSE'S FINAL SPRINT PUTS SAVE AMERICA ACT AND IRAN FUNDING IN PLAY
The budget reconciliation process allows the party in power in Congress to pass sweeping fiscal policy legislation while completely sidelining the other side — in this case, Democrats.
It does so by bypassing the Senate filibuster — which needs 60 votes to overcome — allowing the upper chamber to line up with the House's own simple majority threshold.
Reconciliation 3.0 includes $73 billion for Pentagon and intelligence funding, which is largely tied to replenishing U.S. weapons caches for the Iran war.

U.S. airmen prepare to load GBU-31 munition systems onto F-15E Strike Eagles within the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility Dec. 19, 2025, in support of Operation Hawkeye Strike. (U.S. Air Force Photo/Reuters)
GOP'S $95B DEFENSE PACKAGE SURVIVES CRITICAL HURDLE AMID FISCAL HAWK REVOLT

While Wiles and the other Trump administration leaders articulated their vision for the third reconciliation bill, the entire room bought in and committed to their plan, the source told Fox News Digital.

Further, the defense company leaders spoke favorably about the White House's approach and said they were working hard to advocate for lawmakers on the Hill to pass the House budget resolution before the imminent August recess.

The House has passed a framework with cash targets for relevant committees, but now those committees need to provide details about how that money will be spent. The main players are the House Armed Services Committees and the House Intelligence Committee.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., attends a news conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The president has vigorously advocated to get the deal done.
"I am asking all House Republicans to VOTE YES this week on the Budget Resolution, which is an important first step towards getting a Budget Bill," he said Monday on TRUTH Social.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Smithsonian pushed ‘revolting’ social action training after ‘whiteness’ chart apology: expert
summary: Smithsonian staff co-authored a DEI training toolkit that calls objectivity part of White supremacy, years after the museum apologized for a similar chart.
story: Heritage expert Mike Gonzalez called out the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for the ‘insanity’ of its DEI activism.

Smithsonian staff played a pivotal role in developing what one expert referred to as a "revolting" DEI training guide despite the taxpayer-funded institution previously walking back and apologizing for a similar chart on "whiteness," a series of House hearings this week revealed.

Mike Gonzalez, a DEI and identity politics expert at the Heritage Foundation, testified that, years after the Smithsonian apologized for its controversial "whiteness" chart, the National Museum of American History continued advancing similar concepts through a training guide known as the "Museums as Sites for Social Action" (MASS) toolkit.
Similar to the chart, Gonzalez said the toolkit describes objectivity, individualism, perfectionism and several other concepts as characteristics of White supremacy.
WATCH: ‘SHOCKING’ BEN FRANKLIN SMEAR LEAVES SMITHSONIAN CHIEF WITH ‘NO REGRETS’
In addition to staff members co-authoring the toolkit, Gonzalez said museum leadership kept "indoctrinating staff" for years by holding staff reading groups to study its materials.

"[The] museum kept surreptitiously indoctrinating staff with this trash for three years after the museum apologized for using it, which shows the promises of reform are written in sand," he said in one of the hearings this week.

"This is their own words. The leadership of the Smithsonian says constantly that it wants to use the museum to transform America, for societal transformation. They see history itself as a tool, an instrument to change society."

Anthea Hartig, president of the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, left; Heritage Foundation senior fellow Mike Gonzalez; and Hillsdale College Van Andel Graduate School of Government Dean Matthew Spalding testify during the House Oversight and Government Reform Subcommittee on Delivering on Government Efficiency hearing July 21, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

In 2020, the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture removed and apologized for a chart that described "objective, rational linear thinking" as an aspect of "whiteness" or "white dominant culture," saying, "We erred in including the chart. We have removed it, and we apologize," The Miami Herald reported.

In a viral moment from one of the hearings this week, Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, confronted Smithsonian National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig about a passage in the Museums as Sites for Social Action (MASS Action) toolkit used by the museum that asserts objectivity is part of White supremacy.
In response, Hartig said the museum did not develop the toolkit and asserted, 'We’re not promoting any ideology."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Gonzalez, however, pointed out that the toolkit was co-authored by half a dozen current and former Smithsonian employees, including an NMAH employee, and references Smithsonian materials.
"This is what Marxists do. I think that people who want to truly transform the country seize the cultural institutions in order to mold how people think," he said.
"But wait, there’s more."
'THE VIEW' CO-HOST WHINES SMITHSONIAN HEARINGS ARE ABOUT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION NOT WANTING TO PAY REPARATIONS

The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History is being called out for being "ideologically captured" and presenting woke revisionist history on the weekend of America's 250th birthday. (Kevin Carter)
He pointed to a 2022 Excellence in DEAI Report co-authored by Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch that praises the MASS Action toolkit as a good resource for the dissemination of formal DEI training.

The report states that "one major aspect of the work that takes time is shifting leaders and museum professionals away from white-dominant characteristics of perfection, risk aversion, and conflict avoidance to move toward action."
Addressing the lawmakers present during the hearing, Gonzalez said, "Does anyone in this committee believe that perfection is a White characteristic? The man who runs the museum apparently does."
WATCH: BRANDON GILL CORNERS LAW SCHOOL GATEKEEPER WITH DEI QUESTION SHE WON'T ANSWER

National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig appears with former first lady Jill Biden and Smithsonian Institution Secretary Lonnie Bunch during the presentation of Biden's 2021 inaugural dresses at the Smithsonian Jan. 25, 2023. (Mandel Ngan/AFP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Lonnie Bunch himself agrees with this racist nonsense.

"Once again, I call on Congress to do its duty and take back the Smithsonian from a rogue leadership that now uses it as their own plaything for dangerous ideological games," he continued. "This Insanity has gone on long enough."
Fox News Digital reached out to the Smithsonian Institution and the National Museum of American History for comment.
Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Nevada GOP nominee Carrie Buck says she’s ‘coming to retire Dina Titus’
summary: Carrie Buck sits down at Freedom Fest to discuss her campaign to unseat veteran Democrat incumbent in Las Vegas-based swing district.
story: Carrie Buck discusses housing, immigration, taxes and why she believes voters are ready to move on from Rep. Dina Titus

After flipping a Democrat-leaning state senate district in 2020, Carrie Buck is setting her sights on a bigger target this election cycle: Nevada's first congressional district, an urban Las-Vegas-based district stretching east to the Arizona border.
But it will not be easy to oust Congresswoman Dina Titus, an 8-term veteran with strong ties to organized labor, the tourism industry and the business community.

Nevada state Sen. Carrie Ann Buck, a Henderson Republican, is challenging Democratic Rep. Dina Titus in the state's 1st District. (K.M. Cannon/Las Vegas Review-Journal/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

Recently, Buck sat down with Fox News Digital at Freedom Fest in Las Vegas to discuss her swing district appeal, her background as a teacher and principal and why she believes her take on kitchen table economics will enable her to pull off an upset come election day.
MINIVAN MOM PUTS DEM INCUMBENT ON NOTICE IN TOP GOP TARGET DISTRICT: 'SHE HAS DONE NOTHING FOR US'
First and foremost, Buck is no stranger to challenging Democrats on their own turf.

"Well, in 2020, I flipped a blue district to Republican, and it represents 20% of this [NV-1] district. So, I know I can flip the entire district. People are just tired of my Democrat opponent, and they're ready for change."

U.S. Rep. Dina Titus, D-Nev., listens as she heads a roundtable on heat, convened by the Nevada Conservation League, Chispa Nevada and Climate Power at the Whitney Library Conference Room May 28, 2026, in Las Vegas. (L.E. Baskow/Las Vegas Review-Journal/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
Buck cites her three decades of experience in the Nevada education system as critical to understanding the electorate.

"Well, the past 30 years, I've served in the school system here in Nevada. I was a teacher. … I taught adult ESL, I taught children for years. Then I became a principal of one of the lowest performing schools in the state and moved it to a national Title I school. I won the Milken Award in that time.

"And, so, I've been breathing life into children and families for years. When I knock on doors, when I'm out in the community, people are like, ‘Dr. Buck, you were my principal.’ And, so, I think a lot of people know that I'm going to really deliver for Nevadans in D.C."
Housing affordability is a signature issue for Buck.
She pledges to "ensure that Nevadans have access to lower-cost housing" while also "driving down interest rates so that people can buy whatever house that they want to."
TOP GOP TARGET DINA TITUS FENDS OFF HOUSE PRIMARY CHALLENGERS
Buck also argues that the immigration crisis during the Biden administration was a key driver on the housing affordability issue.
Former President Joe Biden speaks about foreign policy during a speech at the State Department in Washington Jan. 13, 2024. (Susan Walsh/AP Photo)
"I think also what impacted housing is the immigration policies of the Biden years, where they allowed all these people into our country and that drove up [the cost of] all of our low-income housing.
"It depleted it. And, so, now that we're seeing people end up getting deported and going back to their original country, I know that it's definitely driving down prices here."
Buck promises that taking a hard line on the national debt will be a top priority.

"Spending is definitely out of control when we look at the waste of taxpayer dollars, waste, fraud and abuse. When we've seen some of these cases from across the nation, it really is a red alert. We need to make sure that we root that out.

"I just actually saw the vice president is heading up this task force, and they're finding lots of fraud. … We can't just release taxpayer dollars. So, reining in the waste, fraud and abuse and making sure that [government spending] goes to the seniors and the children and the veterans who need it."
Buck is a strong supporter of pathways to citizenship for immigrants, but also maintains a hard line on issues of border security and illegal immigration.
"There is a pathway to citizenship, and I think we need to get people signed up. I've been part of a movement to ensure that people have access to get citizenship. And that's the way, the legal way.

"But coming here illegally, you are breaking laws. Those people need to be deported. We've seen so many victims of crimes by illegal immigrants, and that has to stop. We need to make sure that we have safe communities. I'm a wife of a law enforcement officer and know how important our safe communities and our men and women are working out there in law enforcement."
Water issues remain an enormous concern west of the Mississippi, particularly in Nevada. Buck argues that California could and should play a large role in ensuring Nevadans access to water.
The Hoover Dam is one of the National Park Service's most popular tourist attractions. The federal government is expected to declare a water shortage.  (Ashley Soriano/Fox News)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"For too long, Nevada has been the conservationist. … Our citizens conserve so much water. … All it would take is California to build a basin and hold their rainwater and not release it into the Pacific.
"But they're very selfish neighbors. … We need to make sure that our federal government can maybe step in and build these reservoirs to hold water."
David Unsworth reports on Latin America. You can follow David Unsworth on Twitter @LatinAmerUpdate

title: Read the list: 44 lawmakers included in Jack Smith's text sweep as his legal reckoning grows
summary: Jack Smith's probe secretly seized text messages from 44 lawmakers, including Jim Jordan and Chuck Grassley, tied to January 6 and classified documents.
story: Senators spoke with Fox News Digital about newly released documents that Senate Republicans allege show serious misconduct on part of former special counsel Jack Smith.

Former special counsel Jack Smith’s team obtained and reviewed the contents of text messages exchanged between Trump White House officials and 44 current and former members of Congress, according to Justice Department records released by two Republican-led Senate committees.

The messages were contained in White House records subpoenaed from the National Archives covering Oct. 1, 2020, through Jan. 20, 2021. The Justice Department said Smith’s investigative team "apparently bypassed" a filter team established to screen potentially privileged material before investigators accessed it.

House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, on Wednesday issued a criminal referral for Smith, arguing he misled Congress when he stated he did not obtain or review lawmakers' text messages while carrying out his probes into President Donald Trump.
The referral functions as an invitation for the Justice Department to launch an investigation into Smith's conduct.
JACK SMITH THRUST BACK INTO SPOTLIGHT AT BLANCHE HEARING OVER EXPOSED SENATORS’ MESSAGES
Jack Smith, U.S. special counsel, speaks during a news conference in Washington, D.C., Aug. 1, 2023. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Read the list of 44 lawmakers:

Among the senators targeted in the probe were: Sens. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa; Ron Johnson, R-Wis.; John Cornyn, R-Texas; Lindsey Graham, R-S.C.; Josh Hawley, R-Mo.; Mike Lee, R-Utah; Cory Booker, D-N.J.; Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss.; Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska; David Perdue, R-Ga.; Lamar Alexander, R-Tenn.; Martha McSally, R-Ariz.; Rand Paul, R-Ky.; Rick Scott, R-Fla.; Rob Portman, R-Ohio; Roy Blunt, R-Mo.; Susan Collins, R-Maine; Tim Scott, R-S.C.; Tom Cotton, R-Ark.; and Cory Gardner, R-Colo.

On the House side, the investigation targeted: Reps. Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif.; Steve Scalise, R-La.; Jim Jordan, R-Ohio; Devin Nunes, R-Calif.; Adam Smith, D-Wash.; Andy Biggs, R-Ariz.; Mark Walker, R-N.C.; Bryan Steil, R-Wis.; Dan Newhouse, R-Wash.; Doug Collins, R-Ga.; Dusty Johnson, R-S.D.; Elise Stefanik, R-N.Y.; John Katko, R-N.Y.; Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.; Karen Bass, D-Calif.; Ken Buck, R-Colo.; Lee Zeldin, R-N.Y.; Mario Diaz-Balart, R-Fla.; Mo Brooks, R-Ala.; Morgan Griffith, R-Va.; Rodney Davis, R-Ill.; Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho; Scott Perry, R-Pa.; and Thomas Massie, R-Ky.
Fox News Digital reached out to every current lawmaker named on the list.
Grassley and Johnson, through their senior committee positions, were responsible for the release of the new documents.
Several lawmakers on the list had publicly documented roles in efforts surrounding the 2020 election, including those who have since condemned Smith’s review of their communications.
Sen. Chuck Grassley

As president pro tempore of the Senate, Grassley played a procedural role on Jan. 6, 2021, as Congress moved to certify the results of the 2020 presidential election. The senator, for instance, called the Senate into session before senators moved to the House's chamber to participate in a joint session where the results of each state would be certified.
Prior to Jan. 6, Grassley suggested he may preside over the Senate’s debate on disputes over the 2020 election if Vice President Mike Pence didn’t show up.

"Jack Smith’s criminal investigation of President Trump was a runaway train that had no brakes," Grassley said of his messages being collected. "Based on the information that’s been produced to me and Senator Johnson, Biden DOJ and FBI investigators apparently ignored their own routine investigative protocols to obtain and review work-related messages from me and dozens of my Republican and Democrat colleagues who were outside the scope of the government’s investigation."
Sen. Ron Johnson

In the lead-up to Jan. 6, Johnson joined a group of Republican senators calling for an emergency 10-day audit of disputed election results and saying they would vote against certifying electors from contested states unless such a review occurred.

Documents released by the House Jan. 6 committee in early 2023 reported that Johnson was communicating with the former chairman of the Wisconsin Republican Party about a plan to have the state’s GOP-controlled legislature choose its presidential electors. The senator responded that he had no recollection of the conversation and accused the committee of trying to smear him.

Republicans were intensely critical of the House Jan. 6 committee, arguing that it lacked a meaningful voice for the opposition seeing as then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., selected every member while rejecting the nominations put forward by McCarthy. They also argued that the committee focused too little on security and intelligence failures ahead of the breach of the Capitol.

"This is yet another grotesque example of the Biden administration’s weaponization of the Justice Department," Johnson said of the seized text messages. "Jack Smith’s team acted with impunity as they disregarded their own protocols to obtain and access White House text messages, including messages to and from 44 Members of Congress.
"This is precisely why Chairman Grassley and I have worked to uncover the truth, bring transparency to the American people and hold accountable those who weaponized federal law enforcement."
Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., gestures while addressing Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison during a hearing on Capitol Hill Feb. 16, 2026. (CSPAN)
BIDEN SPECIAL COUNSEL’S 'RUNAWAY TRAIN’ SCOOPED UP SENSITIVE LAWMAKER INFO: 'ABUSE OF POWER'
Sen. Lindsey Graham

In the days after the 2020 election, Graham urged Trump not to concede. He later donated to Trump’s legal defense fund and, as chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, opened inquiries into election procedures in several battleground states and contacted state election officials.
The late South Carolina senator grew frustrated with Trump and his followers as their objections continued to fail in court and fully broke with the movement after the riot on Jan. 6.
"Count me out," he said at the time. "Enough is enough."
Sen. Josh Hawley

Hawley is notable in that he, on Dec. 30, 2020, became the first senator to announce his intention to formally object to Electoral College votes during the certification process. His decision was consequential as federal law required objections from both a representative and a senator to force a debate on the election.
WATCH: HAWLEY FUMES AFTER 4 GOP SENATORS HELP SINK TRUMP-BACKED VOTER ID LAW
Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., talks with reporters in the U.S. Capitol during votes related to the government shutdown Oct. 16, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Trump attempted to call Hawley six times ahead of the Jan. 6 breach, according to White House call logs obtained by the House Jan. 6 select committee, showing that there was a line of communication between the two.

Though some senators abandoned their objections to the 2020 election after the Capitol was breached, Hawley maintained his objections and voted against certifying the results from Arizona and Pennsylvania.
Hawley called the documents released by Grassley and Johnson "more evidence of Biden corruption. Jack Smith illegally scooped up the text messages of Senators — including mine."
Sen. Mike Lee

Text messages turned over by former White House chief of staff Mark Meadows to the House Jan. 6 committee show that Lee discussed possible legal and constitutional avenues for challenging the 2020 election results.

Lee initially told Meadows he supported exhausting every available legal and constitutional remedy to address concerns about the election. By Jan. 3, 2021, however, he warned that the effort "could all backfire badly," according to text messages Meadows turned over to the House Jan. 6 committee.
The senator ultimately voted against sustaining objections to Arizona’s and Pennsylvania's election results.
Mike Lee slammed Smith's collection of text messages this month as "un-American" and argued that it came "uncomfortably close to spying on a coequal, coordinate branch."
Rep. Steve Scalise

Scalise, as House Republican whip, was responsible for convincing representatives to vote in line with the party’s interests, providing a straightforward reason as to why White House staff may have been in contact with him.

Further, a publicly released deposition shows that a Scalise aide communicated with Pence’s legislative affairs director regarding a Jan. 3 call organized by Jordan involving Trump, Meadows and members pressing certification objections.
House Majority Leader Steve Scalise looks on from the floor of the New York Stock Exchange before morning trading April 15. (Adam Gray/Getty Images)
SCALISE URGES PRITZKER TO 'LOOK AT THE MAN IN THE MIRROR' AFTER HE BLAMES TRUMP FOR POLITICAL VIOLENCE
The Louisiana congressman called congressional action the "only remaining recourse" for addressing what he described as improper changes to election laws in several states.
While he condemned rioting, Scalise, like Hawley, ultimately voted to reject Biden’s electoral votes from both Arizona and Pennsylvania.
Rep. Jim Jordan
Jordan participated in efforts to challenge the 2020 election results, including discussions about delaying congressional certification and objecting to electoral votes.

On Jan. 2, the Ohio congressman led a conference call with Trump and other members of Congress to discuss strategies for delaying the Jan. 6 joint session, according to the House Jan. 6 committee’s final report.

Jordan also reportedly had a 10-minute call with Trump on the morning of Jan. 6, according to publicly released phone records. After the breach of the Capitol, Jordan condemned the violence but voted to sustain objections to the electoral results in Arizona and Pennsylvania.

"You can’t do that. As Senator Hawley just said, this is a separation of powers issue," Jordan told Fox News host Sean Hannity earlier this month. "There’s a speech or debate clause. It was supposed to be filtered and screened. It wasn’t. It was just given from the National Archives to Jack Smith’s team."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Smith’s attorneys called the criminal referral "meritless" Thursday in a letter previously obtained by Fox News Digital.

"The House Judiciary Committee’s referral to the Department of Justice of our client Jack Smith is based on a spurious claim that Mr. Smith provided false testimony during his eight-hour deposition on December 17, 2025. The referral is made not because Mr. Smith made a false statement — the letter concedes he did not — but because he did not proactively disclose information that was not responsive to a question asked," the lawyer wrote.

"During his testimony, Mr. Smith provided truthful, responsive answers and candidly discussed his work as Special Counsel. This referral reflects a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system by attacking a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law."
Fox News Digital's Elizabeth Elkind contributed to this report.

title: Trump endorsement fails to clear GOP field as former governor joins South Carolina Senate race
summary: Mark Sanford joined a crowded GOP field challenging Trump-endorsed Darline Graham in South Carolina's special Senate primary set for Aug. 11.
story: Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., discusses the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., and her future in public office after succeeding him on ‘Hannity.’

Former congressman and former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford, a GOP critic of President Donald Trump, launched a Senate bid Thursday, becoming the latest high-profile Republican running for the seat of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham and joins a crowded field against Trump's endorsed candidate.

"We’re at a tipping point, and that’s why I’ve decided to run for the U.S. Senate," Sanford said in a launch video. "I’d ask that you look at my record in Congress and as governor in watching out for your family’s future."

Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed last week to fill the remainder of her late brother's term, announced Monday in an interview on Fox News' "Hannity" she's running for a full six-year term in the Senate. Graham's announcement came three days after she met with Trump at the White House, where the president gave her his "complete and total endorsement" as he encouraged her to run.
But Trump's backing of the late senator's sister isn't stopping other well-known South Carolina Republicans from jumping into the contest.
WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN: CHECK OUT THE FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS ON THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS
Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., arrives to the swearing-in for Darline Graham Nordone as U.S. senator at the U.S. Capitol July 14, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Republican Rep. Ralph Norman, who unsuccessfully campaigned this year for the GOP gubernatorial nomination in the race to succeed term-limited South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, announced his intention to run this past weekend.

Two-term GOP Rep. Russell Fry followed Monday. And businessman Mark Lynch, who lost to Lindsey Graham by nearly 30 points in last month's GOP Senate primary, also announced he'd take another shot at the Republican nomination.
The special Republican Senate primary will be held Aug. 11. If no candidate tops 50%, a runoff election will be held among the top two voter-getters on Aug. 25.
WHAT DARLINE GRAHAM TOLD FOX NEWS' SEAN HANNITY

Former Congressman and former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford is running in next month's special Republican Senate primary in the race to fill the seat of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. (Sean Rayford/Getty Images)

Sanford, who served three terms in the U.S. House in the 1990s, won election as South Carolina governor in 2002 and was re-elected four years later. A rising conservative star in the GOP, he grabbed national attention and derailed his political career with an extramarital affair in 2009. But Sanford made a political comeback, winning election to his old seat in Congress in 2012 and serving three terms.
He briefly launched a long-shot and unsuccessful presidential nomination challenge against Trump in the 2020 primaries.
Known as a fiscally conservative budget hawk, Sanford pointed to the nation's debt as a key motivator behind his decision to launch a Senate campaign.

"Our country is at a financial tipping point, and I can’t sit on the sidelines while Washington adds a trillion dollars to the debt every 100 days," Sanford explained. "I’m worried for our children because, for the first time, America is borrowing from the future faster than we’re building it."
Unlike Sanford, Fry and Norman, who are both Trump allies in the House, are highlighting their support for the president.

"South Carolina doesn't need just another senator. It needs President Trump's strongest ally in the United States Senate. Make no mistake: I will be President Trump’s favorite U.S. Senator, and you will have a MAGA fighter you can count on," Fry wrote in a social media post as he announced his Senate run.
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB
Rep. Russell Fry, R-S.C., arrives for the House Republican Conference caucus meeting at the Capitol Hill Club in Washington May 13, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Fry described himself as a "MAGA warrior" in an accompanying video, which included pictures of him smiling alongside Trump.
Norman emphasized that he's "running to represent the people of South Carolina in the U.S. Senate because we need a fighter who will stand with President Trump and carry on Lindsey Graham’s legacy!"
And pointing to Trump's top legislative priority, he noted, "I want to get the SAVE America Act passed in the Senate!"

Republican Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Rick Scott of Florida, conservatives and staunch Trump allies in the chamber, both cited Norman's support for Trump's election reform bill as they went against the president and endorsed the congressman. Norman is also being backed by the political arm of the powerful conservative group Turning Point USA.

Norman also landed the backing of Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina. The endorsement by Mace, first reported by Fox News Digital, came after the retiring congresswoman, who unsuccessfully ran for governor, announced on Monday she wouldn't run for the Senate.

Besides the president's powerful endorsement, Graham does have the backing of heavy hitters in Congress, including Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., who said, "Darline Graham is an excellent senator. She’ll continue to be an excellent senator, and she has my full support."
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., however, is staying out of the race for now.
Thune said Graham is a "strong candidate," and though she lacked elected experience, he noted she was "very accomplished in her own life."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Sen. Darline Graham Nordone, R-S.C., participates in a ceremonial swearing-in in the Old Senate Chamber at the U.S. Capitol on July 14 in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
"She has a right, like everybody else, to get in that race," Thune said.

Backed by Trump's endorsement and enjoying plenty of name recognition thanks to her well-known last name, pundits view Darline Graham as a frontrunner in the three-week sprint to the Republican primary. And the winner of the GOP nomination will be considered the clear favorite against Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in the general election in the solidly red southeastern state.
Trump's endorsements aren't infallible, but his track record so far this cycle, albeit a couple of setbacks, is impressive.
Veteran Republican strategist and communicator Ryan Williams noted that "the Trump endorsement is a major boost for any candidacy, but it doesn’t necessarily give you a lock on the seat."

"Senate seats in South Carolina do not come up very often, and politics is all about timing. You’ve got to seize the opportunity when it presents itself," Williams told Fox News Digital. "If you’re an aspiring House member in South Carolina, this is your time to run, regardless of whom the president is supporting."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
And Williams, referring to Norman and Fry, noted, "There’s no downside for running. They’re going to run as Trump Republicans, and they’re going to flatter the president on the campaign trail."
That's likely not the case for Sanford, who didn't mention Trump in his social media post or his accompanying campaign launch video.
Fox News' Liz Elkind contributed to this story.

title: Trump's patience 'running out' as Thune fires back over stalled election security bill
summary: Karoline Leavitt says Trump's patience is wearing thin with John Thune over the SAVE America Act as Senate Republicans face a 50-vote math problem.
story: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt warned that President Donald Trump’s patience with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., was running thin as the GOP’s struggles to pass the SAVE America Act.

The fight over President Donald Trump’s SAVE America Act has moved from squabbles within the GOP to the top Senate Republican and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt publicly sniping at one another.
Leavitt suggested Thursday that Trump’s patience was wearing thin with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., over his flagship election security legislation.

"His patience is running out. He wants to see as much of the Save America [Act] passed as possible by the August recess," Leavitt said of the heavy-handed president. "He knows that's what the American people want to see passed.
REPUBLICAN SAYS TRUMP'S TOP ELECTION PRIORITY 'DEAD' IN SENATE AS GOP FRACTURES AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., wasn’t happy with White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and her assertion that the president’s patience was wearing thin with him over the SAVE America Act. (Getty Images )

"And I would just add, you know, the American people … elected overwhelmingly Republicans to lead not just this White House, but also the House and the Senate," she continued. "The House did its job. The Senate needs to do its job, too."

But in the Senate, the political reality looks much different than Leavitt’s assertion that Republicans in the upper chamber weren’t doing enough. Still, Thune has become the dartboard for conservatives, online and at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave., to throw their frustrations over the SAVE America Act at.

The SAVE America Act is universally despised by Senate Democrats, who argue it would disenfranchise millions of Americans from voting. Thune would need Democrats to pass the bill, compared to the House, where Republicans can ram through legislation without Democratic help.
TRUMP'S VOTER ID BILL CATCHES UNLIKELY BREAK AS MCCONNELL REMAINS SIDELINED
Further compounding the issue is the fact that not every Republican is on board with the legislation.

And even though House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and Trump are hoping that Thune and Republicans can pass a version of the SAVE America Act through the party-line budget reconciliation process, which requires 50 votes to work, there’s no guarantee that the support is there.

"Well, maybe she or somebody else ought to get on the phone and get the votes, right? It's 50 around here," Thune said. "So, instead of, you know, pointing the finger at Republicans, they might think about going after the people who are stopping it on the floor, which is the Democrats. And if there are Republicans that they think are gettable, get on the phone. Let's get them to yes."
GOP CIVIL WAR ERUPTS OVER TRUMP'S LATEST AGENDA PUSH AS KEY REPUBLICANS THREATEN TO SINK MEGABILL

In the Senate, Republicans are growing increasingly frustrated with the expectations surrounding the bill that aren’t feasible given the math problem bogging the legislation down in the upper chamber.
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., makes his way to a vote in the U.S. Capitol April 30, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc)

Thune is considering using the reconciliation process to keep the government open, too, in the event that Democrats renege in ongoing negotiations to craft a short-term funding deal as the typical government funding process struggles to move forward.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., one of the most vocal opponents of the SAVE America Act, said Republicans should turn to reconciliation to fund the government and that some were "being dishonest to the American people to say that we need SAVE Act passed because there's no way on God's green Earth it can be implemented by the election."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
When asked about Leavitt’s comments against Thune, Tillis dug in.
"I have 1,000% confidence in Thune, and anybody in the White House who thinks he's not a good leader isn't qualified for their job," he said.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: AI builds virtual homes where robots learn from their mistakes
summary: SceneSmith uses AI agents powered by GPT-5.2 to build detailed 3D environments where robots practice tasks and expose faulty plans before real homes.
story: Salamanca High School in New York introduces Sally, a 5'2" humanoid robot, as a teaching assistant for upper grades. Sally features lifelike silicone skin and designed facial expressions. The school district emphasizes that the $57,000 robot won't replace human teachers and operates on a closed AI system with no student data transmitted to manufacturers.

Ask a robot to put a coffee mug in the cabinet, and you quickly see how complicated an ordinary chore can become. You know where the mug belongs. You can step around a chair, avoid the clutter on the counter and open the right cabinet without giving it much thought. A robot has to work through every part of that process.

That helps explain why today's robots can look impressive during a demonstration but still struggle with basic jobs around a home or factory. They need experience in many different rooms and situations before they can work reliably. Teaching them everything in the physical world takes time and plenty of hands-on supervision.

Researchers at MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and Toyota Research Institute believe virtual training could help. Their system, called SceneSmith, uses AI agents to create detailed 3D indoor environments from simple text prompts. Robots can then practice tasks and expose weak action plans inside those AI-generated spaces before they enter a real home or workplace.

WOULD YOU TRUST A TINY DENTAL ROBOT?
Robots can test weak action plans inside AI-generated homes before operating around people and property. (SceneSmith)
Why AI virtual homes matter for robot training

Robots learn through experience. However, engineers cannot easily stage every room layout or object arrangement a machine may encounter. Physical testing also requires someone to reset the scene after each attempt. A tipped chair or misplaced bottle can change the next test. Meanwhile, a failed movement may damage the robot or something nearby.

Simulation offers a safer alternative. A robot can repeat a task without breaking a dish or tying up a real workspace. Still, many earlier simulation systems created rooms that felt sparse. They often lacked the clutter, movable furniture and physical details found in everyday spaces. SceneSmith makes those training environments feel much closer to the real world.
Other developers are also using AI video technology to speed up humanoid robot training, turning small amounts of real footage into synthetic training environments.
How SceneSmith builds AI virtual homes

SceneSmith starts with a simple written request. A researcher could ask for a garage with a car and workbench, then add tires in the corner and a ladder against the wall. From there, three AI agents powered by GPT-5.2 work together to build the space. A designer starts creating the room. A critic checks whether everything looks realistic. An orchestrator manages the back-and-forth and decides when the design is ready.

SceneSmith builds each environment one layer at a time. It starts with the floor plan and furniture, then adds objects to the walls and ceiling. Smaller items that a robot can pick up or move come last. The critic also catches choices that feel out of place. For example, it might suggest removing a bathtub from the living room. The orchestrator can even send the project back a few steps when part of the design needs more work.

Once the agents agree, SceneSmith adds the physics that control how objects move and react. The result gives researchers a working virtual room where a robot can open cabinets and handle objects instead of a 3D scene that only looks realistic.
SceneSmith creates objects robots can use

A robot needs more than realistic scenery. It needs objects that respond when touched. SceneSmith can place cabinets with working doors. It can also create movable objects and estimate physical properties such as mass or friction. Those details affect how an item reacts when a robot grabs, pushes or drops it.

For standard objects, the system can use a text-to-image-to-3D process. It retrieves articulated items with moving parts from a curated library. This approach keeps cabinet doors and drawers functional inside the simulator. The system also checks for overlapping objects and lets gravity settle them into stable positions.

Researchers reported that 96% of objects remained stable during simulation. Fewer than 2% of object pairs collided with one another. That work matters because a robot cannot learn much from a virtual kitchen where cups float or furniture sinks into the floor.
Better virtual practice could also support advances like this new AI brain that helps robots move more like humans, especially when a task requires precise hand movements.
HUMANOID ROBOT CLEANS FIRST US APARTMENT
MIT researchers used SceneSmith to generate more than 1,300 virtual spaces, including bedrooms, hotels and cluttered specialty rooms. (SceneSmith)
SceneSmith created more than 1,300 training spaces

The researchers used SceneSmith to generate more than 1,300 scenes. The collection included familiar spaces such as bedrooms and hotels. It also produced unusual settings, including a pottery store and a Minecraft-themed gaming room. Some scenes contained up to six times more items than those from earlier methods. As a result, robots can encounter the type of clutter that makes real-world tasks difficult.

A robot might need to move a soda can from a shelf to a table. Another task could involve placing a cup in the sink. Each scene changes the surroundings, so the robot cannot depend on one carefully staged layout. That variety gives engineers a better way to see whether a robot's plan works beyond a single demonstration.
AI virtual homes can expose faulty robot plans

In robotics, a policy tells a machine how to act based on what it observes. SceneSmith gives researchers a way to test those policies across many environments. The team generated 100 evaluation scenes covering four manipulation tasks. A robot policy attempted each chore in simulation. Then, an AI evaluator checked the result using simulator data and visual observations.

The evaluator reached 99.7% agreement with human labels. That result suggests researchers could use the system to screen robot attempts at scale without manually judging every run. The headline's phrase "learn from their mistakes" needs one important distinction. SceneSmith reveals where a policy fails. Engineers can use those failures to revise later versions of the robot's behavior. In this study, the system focused on scene generation and automatic evaluation rather than continuous self-retraining after every mistake.
Researchers tested whether the virtual homes worked

A virtual room can look realistic to a person and still behave poorly during robot training. Therefore, the team tested SceneSmith through physical interaction inside the simulator. Researchers placed an independently trained robot policy into generated scenes. The policy predated SceneSmith and had never trained on its environments or assets.

In one demonstration, the robot moved an apple from a bowl to a cutting board after receiving a language instruction. The team also teleoperated a robot through the virtual spaces. Researchers guided it as it opened cabinets and put away bottles. These tests showed that the environments could support more than visual inspection. Together, the demonstrations provide early evidence that SceneSmith's rooms can support useful robotics experiments.
People preferred SceneSmith's virtual rooms

The researchers asked 205 people to compare SceneSmith with earlier scene-generation methods. SceneSmith recorded an average 92% win rate for realism. It also earned a 91% average win rate for following the original prompt.

In practical terms, participants usually thought its rooms looked more believable and matched the request more closely. Those results support the visual side of the system. However, robot performance remains the more important test. SceneSmith's ability to combine realistic design with usable physics gives the project its strongest advantage.
ROBOT SOCCER PLAYER DENTS WALL WITH TERRIFYING KICKS
MIT’s SceneSmith uses artificial intelligence to build realistic 3D homes where robots can safely practice everyday tasks. (SceneSmith)
SceneSmith still faces a major speed problem

Detailed virtual rooms take time to build. MIT says SceneSmith may need several hours to produce one scene because the AI agents create and inspect many objects. More computing power could speed up that process. Even so, generating a large training library would require substantial resources.

The current system also has limited support for deformable objects such as sponges. These materials change shape when touched, which makes them harder to reproduce in simulation. The researchers hope larger 3D libraries will help them expand that capability.

Real-world testing will still play a vital role. Homes contain unpredictable people and objects that wear down or break. Simulation can reduce risky trial and error, but engineers must still prove that robots behave safely outside a digital room.
What this means to you

A future household robot could practice inside hundreds or even thousands of virtual rooms before it ever rolls into your kitchen. That gives developers more chances to catch a bad move or weak action plan while the robot remains inside a simulator. SceneSmith can also expose a robot to rooms filled with different furniture, objects and layouts. That matters because your kitchen will look nothing like the carefully arranged space where a robot first learned a task.
That kind of preparation could eventually help machines like this home robot designed to cook, clean and handle the clutter and surprises found in everyday homes.

The technology remains in the research stage, and robots will still need plenty of testing in the physical world. Still, SceneSmith tackles a problem robot makers need to solve: How do you prepare a machine for homes where chairs move, counters get cluttered and almost nothing stays in the same place?
Kurt's key takeaways

SceneSmith gives robots a safe place to get things wrong. Engineers can spot a bad move inside a crowded virtual home before the machine risks damaging something or moving too close to a person. What makes this system interesting is that the rooms actually work like physical spaces. Cabinets open, objects move and robots can interact with what is around them. The biggest drawback is speed. Building one detailed scene can take hours. Still, these AI-generated environments could help developers catch more problems before a robot ever enters your home.

title: Trump launches Gold Eagle to hunt cyber flaws with AI
summary: The White House Gold Eagle program uses Anthropic's Claude Mythos to hunt software vulnerabilities, but major questions remain about oversight and access.
story: Matt Shumer, co-founder and CEO of OthersideAI, details Anthropic's new AI model, Mythos, on 'The Sunday Briefing'. The model's "emergent capabilities" to find software vulnerabilities autonomously raised alarms, prompting Anthropic to restrict public access. Shumer explains the proactive move of granting major companies and the US government early access to Mythos for cyber defense, anticipating future threats to critical infrastructure and national security.

Most of us tap Update Now and move on. However, a lot happens before that security patch reaches your phone or computer. Researchers must find the flaw. Someone needs to confirm it. Then the developer has to create a fix that will not cause a new problem.

Now, artificial intelligence can uncover software weaknesses much faster. That sounds promising, but it can also create a flood of vulnerability reports. Worse, attackers can use similar AI tools to hunt for the same openings.

The Trump administration wants to help defenders move first. The White House just announced the Gold Eagle AI cybersecurity clearinghouse. Officials say the program has already started receiving and prioritizing vulnerability reports.

Gold Eagle will connect federal agencies with private companies, critical infrastructure operators and open-source software teams. Its goal is to uncover serious flaws faster and coordinate the work needed to patch them.
AI CHATBOTS TAKE HEAT OVER LEFT-WING BIAS: ‘NO LONGER BE CONSIDERED NEUTRAL’
AI tools can help defenders find dangerous software weaknesses faster, but attackers may use similar technology to target the same flaws. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

What is the Gold Eagle AI cybersecurity clearinghouse?

Gold Eagle is a federal coordination center for software vulnerabilities. The Treasury Department leads the effort with support from CISA and other federal partners. President Trump ordered the creation of the clearinghouse through Executive Order 14409 on June 2, 2026. The order directed Treasury to work with the National Cyber Director and other agencies.

Gold Eagle must coordinate vulnerability scanning and reduce duplicated work. It will also help validate findings before teams spend time fixing them. Finally, the program will support the distribution of patches once they are ready. The White House calls Gold Eagle a "force multiplier." In other words, the government wants each participating security team to accomplish more by sharing reliable information.

Gold Eagle does not replace the developers who maintain the affected software. Instead, it creates a central place where government and industry can coordinate their response. That distinction is important. Finding a bug does not automatically fix it. Developers still need to understand the weakness and build a safe update.
How Gold Eagle uses AI to find cyber vulnerabilities

AI models can review large amounts of computer code quickly. They can also examine how software reacts when someone sends it unusual commands or unexpected data. That speed may help researchers uncover weaknesses that survived years of conventional testing.

A senior White House official said closed-source AI models will participate in Gold Eagle's vulnerability work. That includes Anthropic's Claude Mythos, which the company designed for advanced cybersecurity research. Anthropic says Mythos-class models can find software vulnerabilities and develop ways to exploit them. The company also warns that those abilities could make attacks easier if the models fall into the wrong hands.

That creates an uncomfortable reality. The same AI that can help protect a system may also help someone break into it. Therefore, Gold Eagle's success will depend on more than the model's ability to find bugs. The program must control who receives the details and how quickly developers get a warning.
Why Gold Eagle wants to stop duplicate security scans

Imagine several repair crews checking the same water pipe while another leak goes unnoticed. Cybersecurity teams can face a similar problem. Several organizations may scan the same popular software without knowing that another team already found the flaw. Meanwhile, less visible software may receive little attention.

Gold Eagle aims to coordinate those searches. It can help participating teams avoid repeating work and direct their attention toward software that still needs review. The clearinghouse will also try to cut through low-quality reports. AI models can generate convincing findings that turn out to be harmless or inaccurate.

As a result, human validation remains essential. Security engineers need to reproduce the reported flaw and confirm that it creates a real risk. After that, developers must test the repair. They also need to release the update without breaking the product for existing users.
REDHOOK ANDROID MALWARE CAN QUIETLY HIJACK YOUR PHONE
The Trump administration’s Gold Eagle program uses artificial intelligence to help uncover software flaws and coordinate security patches. (iStock; Rob Newell - CameraSport via Getty Images)
How VINCE handles Gold Eagle vulnerability reports

Gold Eagle will use technology developed with Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute. The system is called the Vulnerability Information and Coordination Environment, or VINCE. Carnegie Mellon's CERT Coordination Center already uses VINCE to accept vulnerability reports and communicate with affected software vendors.

Gold Eagle can use that platform as an intake point for AI-discovered vulnerabilities. Reports can then move through validation and coordination before details become public. This controlled process matters because revealing a serious vulnerability too early can give attackers a head start. Ideally, the software company receives enough time to prepare a patch before technical details spread.

However, several operational questions remain unanswered. The administration has not publicly identified every company participating in Gold Eagle. It has also released few details about daily oversight or the way sensitive reports will move between participants. The government has not said how many findings have resulted in completed patches either.
Why open-source software matters to Gold Eagle

Open-source code sits inside a huge range of commercial products. It can power parts of a browser or business platform without the average user ever knowing its name. However, many open-source projects operate with limited resources. Some rely heavily on maintainers who contribute their time alongside other jobs.

AI could help those teams find dangerous flaws. At the same time, it could overwhelm them with reports that require careful review. Gold Eagle may offer a useful filter. The clearinghouse could validate a report before sending it to a project that lacks a large security department.

It could also connect maintainers with government or industry engineers who can help assess the problem. Anthropic has already worked with open-source groups through Project Glasswing. The company says its partners used Mythos Preview to find more than 10,000 high or critical-severity vulnerabilities. Those figures come from Anthropic and do not represent Gold Eagle's results. Still, those findings show why the government expects AI-generated vulnerability reports to arrive at a much greater scale.
Anthropic's Mythos shows the risks of powerful cyber AI

The government's recent handling of Claude Mythos 5 shows how sensitive these capabilities have become. On June 12, 2026, the U.S. government applied export controls to Mythos 5 and Claude Fable 5. Anthropic suspended access because it could not immediately verify the nationality of every user.

The government lifted those restrictions on June 30. Anthropic restored Mythos 5 access on July 1 to a selected group of approved U.S. organizations. Anthropic currently limits Mythos 5 to vetted partners because the model could support defensive research or harmful activity.
CyberGuy previously took a closer look at how Anthropic's Mythos AI changed cybersecurity and why its ability to uncover thousands of hidden software flaws is raising concern.

Gold Eagle is betting that controlled access can give defenders an advantage. However, other advanced models will continue improving. That means Gold Eagle will need to move quickly. A flaw loses much of its defensive value once an attacker independently discovers it.
Gold Eagle still faces major questions

The idea behind Gold Eagle makes sense. Security teams should share validated findings and avoid wasting time on duplicate scans. However, coordination can become slow when too many organizations must approve each decision.

Gold Eagle will need clear rules for who validates a vulnerability. It also needs a reliable way to decide which reports deserve immediate attention. Transparency will matter too. The government should eventually publish useful performance information without revealing dangerous technical details.

For example, it could report how many findings were validated and how quickly affected developers received them. It could also show how many vulnerabilities led to released patches. The program faces a legal deadline as well. Its information-sharing process relies on protections in the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015.

Congress temporarily extended that law through September 30, 2026. The administration says a lapse could undermine the cooperation Gold Eagle needs from private companies. Companies may hesitate to share sensitive information when they feel uncertain about legal protections. That could weaken the clearinghouse before it has time to prove itself.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
Gold Eagle aims to help security teams turn verified software flaws into patches before cybercriminals can exploit them. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to protect yourself from newly discovered security flaws

Gold Eagle works mostly behind the scenes. However, the patch still has to reach your device. You also need to install it. Here are several ways to reduce your exposure while companies work to close newly discovered flaws.

Enable automatic updates for your phone and computer. You should also update your browser and regularly used apps. Many software updates close security holes. Automatic installation reduces the time that a known flaw remains open on your device. However, review major operating system upgrades before installing them on a device you rely on for critical work. A short delay may make sense when an update has widely reported compatibility problems. For step-by-step help, see CyberGuy's guide on how to update all of your devices and keep them safe at cyberguy.com

Your router may not display update reminders as visibly as your phone. The same problem can affect security cameras and other connected devices. Open the manufacturer's app or support page and check for firmware updates. Some newer routers let you enable automatic updates. Also, change any default administrator password that came with the device. For additional router checks, see how Russian hackers hijacked old Wi-Fi routers and the steps you can take to protect yours.

A device can continue working after its manufacturer stops supporting it. However, newly discovered vulnerabilities may remain unpatched. Check the manufacturer's support policy when you own an older router or connected product. Consider replacing the device when it reaches the end of its security-update period. CISA warns that unsupported network equipment can increase an organization's attack surface.

A real vulnerability can inspire fake update messages. Criminals may send an email that claims you must download an urgent security patch. Do not install software from an unexpected email or text message. Instead, open your device settings or the manufacturer's official app. You can also visit its verified support page directly. CISA recommends downloading patches from validated sources.

Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious files that try to exploit a weakness on your computer. Keep the protection active and allow it to update automatically. New detection information helps the software recognize recently identified threats. Still, antivirus software cannot make an unsupported device safe. It works best as one layer alongside regular updates. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

A current backup can help you recover if malware damages your files or ransomware locks them. Use a trusted cloud backup service or an external drive. When using an external drive, disconnect it after the backup finishes so malware cannot easily reach it. Finally, confirm that your backup is working. A backup you have never checked may fail when you need it most. For help choosing a method, check out our article on how to back up your devices the right way.
Kurt's key takeaways

What stands out to me is how quickly AI is changing the cyber fight. It can help researchers uncover serious software flaws faster, but finding the problem is only half the battle. Someone still has to confirm it, build the fix and get that update onto your device before criminals take advantage. Gold Eagle could make that process less scattered by giving government agencies, private companies and open-source developers one place to coordinate. That could save valuable time when a major vulnerability appears. The real test will be what happens next. We need to see whether Gold Eagle can protect sensitive findings and help turn them into patches people actually receive. There is also a legal deadline coming in September that could affect how freely companies share threat information. For now, do not wait for a federal program to protect every device you own. Keep your software updated and take a closer look at older routers or smart devices that may no longer receive security fixes.

title: Fake password-manager alerts could put your vault at risk
summary: LastPass warns of a phishing campaign using lookalike domains and a fake DocuSign page to trick users into downloading dangerous software.
story: Halimah Delaine Prado, Google General Counsel, reveals the rise of AI-powered phishing scams originating from China's 'outsider enterprise.' She explains how these criminals use artificial intelligence to create highly convincing fake websites, impersonating trusted brands like T-Mobile to defraud hundreds of thousands of Americans, causing millions in losses. Prado highlights Google's strategy to combat these evolving threats.

You open your inbox and see a message about updated security policies. Nothing about it screams scam. The email looks polished, the wording sounds official and the button promises a quick way to review the changes. That is exactly what makes it dangerous.
LastPass is warning users about a newly identified phishing campaign that uses lookalike domains and a fake DocuSign page to lure people into downloading suspicious software.

The good news is that LastPass says its systems were not affected. The bad news is that scammers are counting on you to trust the logo, overlook the web address and click before taking a closer look. Here is what to watch for before one routine-looking email puts your entire password vault at risk.

FBI HELPS TAKE DOWN AI PHISHING RING
Scammers are impersonating LastPass with fake policy emails that lead users to a fraudulent DocuSign page and suspicious software download. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
LastPass phishing scam starts with a routine policy email

The phishing email comes from hello@lastpassnewsletter.com. Its known subject line reads, "Action Required: Review Updated LastPass Security Policies." Inside, the message claims LastPass has made service policy changes. It mentions enhanced SaaS monitoring. It also claims administrators can reset master passwords and that the admin console has improved.

Those details make the email sound like a real company notice. However, the sending domain belongs to the attackers. LastPass says lastpassnewsletter[.]com has no affiliation with the company. The email includes a Review & Access Terms button. That button creates the next layer of the trap.
Fake LastPass page sends you to a DocuSign lookalike

Clicking the button sends you to lastpasscompliance[.]com. The landing page copies the look of DocuSign and claims a document is ready for review. That choice makes sense from a scammer's perspective. Many people receive electronic signature requests at work or while handling personal paperwork. A familiar layout can lower your guard before you inspect the web address.

We have seen the same trust trick in other fake DocuSign email scams. The brand name gives the request a sense of legitimacy, even when the sender and domain do not match. LastPass says Microsoft Defender for Office 365 and Cloudflare classified the phishing site as malicious. The page also prompted visitors to download software that claimed to work on Windows and macOS.

LastPass was still investigating the download when it published its warning. Therefore, you should treat the file as dangerous and avoid opening it. The site also displayed a live support chat box, although it was unclear whether the chat worked. The malicious page had gone offline by the time the campaign was reported. However, attackers can quickly replace blocked domains with new ones.
Similar Bitwarden emails widen the warning

LastPass users are not the only targets. Bitwarden customers have received similar messages from hello@bitwardennewsletter.com. Those emails directed recipients to bitwardencompliance[.]com. The matching format suggests attackers may be reusing the same campaign structure across password manager brands.

That matters because password manager customers present an attractive target. One stolen master password could put many saved accounts at risk. Multi-factor authentication may still block access, depending on your security settings.

A password manager remains valuable protection. In fact, autofill can help expose a fake website because the manager should recognize the legitimate domain. You can compare current options in our guide to the best password managers for 2026 at cyberguy.com
LastPass users have faced several phishing lures in 2026

This campaign follows other LastPass-themed phishing attempts from earlier this year. In January, fake messages warned that users had only 24 hours to back up their vaults before maintenance. Then, a March campaign used fabricated email threads about unauthorized account access.

Both approaches relied on urgency to push people into acting before they verified the message. The new compliance notice uses a calmer approach. It looks like paperwork rather than a crisis. That may make it especially effective because policy updates feel normal and boring.
REDHOOK ANDROID MALWARE CAN QUIETLY HIJACK YOUR PHONE
Ways to stay safe from the LastPass phishing scam
The fraudulent page impersonates DocuSign and prompts visitors to download suspicious software for Windows or macOS. (LastPass)
A few careful steps can keep one convincing email from turning into a much larger problem.
Delete the message or report it as phishing. Do not reply. Avoid opening its links or downloading the file it offers.
Use the official LastPass app or type lastpass.com into your browser. Check for account notices after you sign in through the trusted route.

Lookalike domains often add a trusted brand name to words such as "newsletter" or "compliance." Check the website address before the first slash. A legitimate LastPass address should end in lastpass.com, such as support.lastpass.com, rather than merely containing the word "LastPass."

A password manager may refuse to fill your credentials on a fake domain. Treat that as a warning. Do not copy and paste the password to get around it. Instead, close the page and access your account through the official app or website.

Use a trusted device and go directly to LastPass. Change the master password immediately. Then review your vault for unexpected activity, as LastPass recommends. Next, change passwords for sensitive accounts stored in the vault if you see signs of access. Start with email, financial accounts, cloud storage and social media. Use a different password for every account.
AMAZON RECALL TEXT SCAM COMES WITH RED FLAGS
The scam relies on polished security notices, familiar branding and misleading web addresses to lower users’ defenses. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Do not open software offered by a security notice you reached through email. If you already opened the file, disconnect the affected device from the internet. Then use strong antivirus software to inspect it. Our current best antivirus protection guide at cyberguy.com can help you compare tools that block malicious websites and dangerous downloads. It also covers protection against malware. You can also follow these steps after you clicked a suspicious email and entered information.

Enable multi-factor authentication for your password manager and other important accounts. An authenticator app or security key can add a barrier if someone steals your password. However, never approve a login request you did not initiate. A second security step only helps when you treat unexpected prompts as a warning.

Scammers often use information from data broker sites to make phishing emails feel more personal. That could include your phone number, home address, relatives or past employers. A data removal service can help find and remove some of that information from people-search websites. It will not secure a compromised password manager, but it may give scammers fewer details to use in future attacks. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com
Forward questionable LastPass-branded emails to abuse@lastpass.com. LastPass says no one from the company will ever ask for your master password.
Kurt's key takeaways

What makes this scam dangerous is how normal the email looks. Most people expect password manager alerts to sound urgent. This one arrives dressed up as a boring policy update, which may make you less likely to question it. The biggest red flag is the web address. A company name inside a domain does not mean the company owns it. Before entering a master password or downloading anything, close the email and open the password manager directly. Your master password protects everything stored in your vault. Treat any request for it like someone asking for the keys to your house.

title: Robot bird swims underwater then flies away
summary: MIT and EPFL researchers built an 8.8-ounce robotic bird that flies, dives underwater and launches back into the air using only flapping wings.
story: Fox News correspondent Brooke Taylor meets Saronic CEO Dino Mavrookas to unveil the future of modern warfare with an exclusive look at autonomous drone boats. These innovative vessels are capable of military rescues without putting service members in danger, marking a significant milestone. Mavrookas emphasizes the ability to build thousands of these cost-effective, complex mission-ready ships, including the new 52-foot Mirage.

Watching a diving bird vanish beneath the water can feel almost unreal. One moment it cruises through the sky. Seconds later, it swims after prey before returning to the air. Around 100 bird species can move between those two environments. Engineers have found that natural ability incredibly difficult to recreate at a small scale.

Now, researchers at MIT and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne, known as EPFL, have built a robotic bird that can complete the entire journey. The 8.8-ounce robot flies, plunges into water and swims below the surface. Then it launches back into the air using the same set of flapping wings.
NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL
Researchers say the $300 robot marks the first bird-scale machine to complete an air-to-water-to-air cycle using flapping wings alone. (Raphael Zufferey)
According to the research team, it marks the first bird-scale robot to complete that full cycle through flapping motion alone. The research appeared in the journal Science.
